At larger radii, one particularly striking feature is a well-defined dust lane visible in the color image (top panel of Figure 7), which extends over $\rm\sim 2.6~kpc$ if deprojected, assuming that it lies in the disk plane. This feature is also apparent in the color, $A_{V}$ , and $C_{f}\times N$ maps, indicating a localized enhancement in gas and dust. While the narrow dust lane is most prominent, we see enhanced Na I D absorption and $A_{V}$ behind the dust lane that extends over $\sim 120^{\circ}$ in azimuth. There may also be a feature located diametrically opposite from the dust lane, but we see a hint of it only in the Na I D map and not in the image, color, or $A_{V}$ maps.

The non-axisymmetric distribution of gas and dust likely points to a recent minor merger or accretion event that deposited cold gas into the system. We will discuss this interpretion further in Section VII. The asymmetries in the gas distribution are robust to the assumed ${\rm[Na/Fe]^{*}}$ . Its value mainly determines whether the asymmetries contain nearly all of the gas in the outer galaxy beyond about 2 kpc (if ${\rm[Na/Fe]^{*}}=+0.6$ ), or whether they coexist with a smooth component (if ${\rm[Na/Fe]^{*}}=0$ ).

The presence of a smooth gas component is not necessarily inconsistent with the lack of dust attenuation observed in much of the outer galaxy. We expect Na I D absorption to be more sensitive tracer at low gas column densities. In the Milky Way, $\rm N_{H}/A_{V}\approx(2.08\pm 0.02)\times 10^{21}~cm^{-2}~mag^{-1}$ [155]. We therefore expect a minimally low $A_{\rm V}\lesssim 0.1$ mag where $N_{\rm H}\lesssim 2\times 10^{20}$ cm-2. Using the conversion provided by Moretti et al. [81], this corresponds to $\rm N_{Na~I}\lesssim 6\times 10^{12}$ cm-2. Thus the lower values in the $C_{f}\times N$ map (Figure 7, panel D) are expected to correspond to negligible attenuation.

### IV.2 Gas Kinematics

From the pPXF fits, we mapped the stellar velocity $V_{\rm star}$ (Figure 7, panel B), revealing a clear rotation pattern. The Na I D velocity field (Figure 7, panel C) also exhibits a rotation pattern, and the kinematic axis is closely aligned with that of the stars. This indicates that the neutral gas is in situ ISM, at least mainly. Nuclear outflows, as have been found in some younger quiescent galaxies at a similar redshift [34, 10, 69, 90], are expected to escape perpendicular to the disk [6, 25, 5, 126]. This would result in velocity field with a kinematic axis orthogonal to the stars, which is clearly not observed in MRG-M0138.

Figure 8 further illustrates the relationship between the gas and stellar kinematics. Overall, the velocity of the gas is correlated with that of the stars, but its rotation speed along a given sight line is slower. The relationship between the velocities for [Na/Fe]* = 0 is characterized by a linear fit,

$$ {V_{\rm gas}=(0.70\pm 0.01)\times V_{\rm star}-(26\pm 3)\rm~km~s^{-1}}, $$

while for [Na/Fe]* = +0.6,

$$ {V_{\rm gas}=(0.50\pm 0.02)\times V_{\rm star}-(68\pm 5)\rm~km~s^{-1}}. $$

Quantitatively, therefore, the velocity lag depends on the partitioning of the absorption between stars and gas and thus the assumed ${\rm[Na/Fe]^{*}}$ . If a higher fraction of the gas is located in the bulge compared to the stars, then the gas along a given sight line would have more bulge-like kinematics than the stars. And based on our stellar dynamical models [87], this would produce lower gas velocities. Small-scale turbulence in the gas could also provide pressure support that reduces the rotation speed required to maintain equilibrium. We will discuss the kinematics further in Section VII.

In addition to the rotation speed lag, the linear fits suggest a systematic zero-point offset between the stellar and gas velocities. In principle, this could indicate a modest, galaxy-wide blueshift of the gas, potentially resulting from an outflowing component that is superposed on the dominant in situ component. However, the magnitude of the zero-point offset depends on the assumed [Na/Fe]* and is comparable to the $\sim 40$ km s-1 velocity uncertainty for NIRSpec observations with the medium-resolution gratings.44 4 https://jwst-docs.stsci.edu/jwst-calibration-status/nirspec-calibration-status/nirspec-mos-calibration-status Consequently we refrain from drawing strong conclusions about the origin of this potential velocity offset.

In Figure 8, we highlight the regions corresponding to the dust lane and the the central off-center clump of gas and dust. We find that these features do not display any peculiar velocities relative to the surrounding gas. Together with the global kinematic alignment of the stars and gas, this suggests that if the gas in MRG-M0138 was accreted, its angular momentum was either already nearly aligned with the galaxy disk, or it has had sufficient time to settle into corotation. We will examine the timescale for this kinematic settling and its connection to star-formation history of MRG-M0138 in Sections V and VII.

### IV.3 Integrated Gas Mass Estimate

As discussed in Section I, measuring the gas mass in high-redshift quiescent galaxies is difficult. Na I D has been used to infer mass outflow rates from massive, high-redshift galaxies (see Section I) and to draw connections to quenching, so tests of the mass estimates are important. In MRG-M0138, we have the opportunity to compare gas mass estimates derived from two methods: Na I D absorption and a prior dust continuum detection [149].

To estimate the gas mass of MRG-M0138, we use our maps of the Na I column density ( $N_{\rm Na~I}$ ) and covering fraction ( $C_{f}$ ). Although $N_{\rm Na~I}$ is known to correlate linearly with the neutral hydrogen column density, $N_{\rm H}=N_{\rm H~I}+2N_{\rm H_{2}}$ [43, e.g.,], the ratio depends on the physical conditions in the gas. We use the empirical conversion from Moretti et al. [81]:

$$ \log N_{\text{H I}}=\log N_{\text{Na I}}+7.5 $$

This calibration was derived from a detailed study of an outflow from a massive galaxy at $z=2.4$ that happens to intersect the line of sight to a bright background quasar [99]. The favorable geometry enabled precise measurements of the relative abundances of metals and hydrogen in the neutral phase of the outflowing gas. The outflow is measured to have a molecular hydrogen fraction of $f=0.27$ [122]. Based on this, we derive and apply a slight modification of the Moretti et al. [81] relation, $\log N_{\rm H}=\log N_{\rm H~I}/(1-f)=\log N_{\rm Na~I}+7.6$ .

We integrated the derived $C_{f}\times N_{\rm H}$ map in the source plane, accounting for the area subtended by each spatial bin using the lensing model. Under the assumption of a symmetric distribution, an absorbing gas parcel typically lies in front of half of the stars along its sightline. We roughly account for the star–gas geometry by multiplying the resulting absorption-based neutral hydrogen masses $M_{\rm H}$ by a factor of 2. This yields $M_{\rm H}=4.9^{+3.7}_{-1.1}\times 10^{7}~\rm M_{\odot}$ for the average of the G140M and G235M data sets, assuming [Na/Fe]* = 0. Adopting models with enhanced [Na/Fe]* = +0.6 lowers the inferred neutral hydrogen mass to $M_{\rm H}\approx 1.7\times 10^{7}~\rm M_{\odot}$ .

We estimate the neutral gas mass fraction as

$$ f_{\rm gas}=1.4\times\frac{M_{\text{H}}}{\rm M_{\star}}, $$

where $M_{\text{H}}$ is the mass of atomic and molecular hydrogen, the factor 1.4 accounts for the mass of He [130, e.g.,], and $M_{\star}$ is the stellar mass of the galaxy (Section II). We find a gas fraction of $f_{\rm gas}=0.031^{+0.023}_{-0.008}\%$ assuming [Na/Fe]*= 0.

We compare our gas mass fraction to that presented by Whitaker et al. [149] based on a detection of MRG-M0138 at 1.3 mm, on the Rayleigh–Jeans tail of the dust emission. By assuming a molecular gas-to-dust mass ratio $\delta_{\rm GDR}=100$ , they reported a molecular gas fraction of $f_{\text{H}_{2}}=M_{\rm H_{2}}/\rm M_{\star}=0.6\pm 0.1\%$ . This is $\gtrsim 12\times$ higher than our Na-based estimate of $f_{\rm gas}$ , where the lower limit indicates that we have used the $1\sigma$ upper limit on $f_{\rm gas}$ . A greater discrepancy would be obtained if we were to assume [Na/Fe]* = +0.6 or add any H I to the $f_{\rm H_{2}}$ estimate. Additionally, Gobat et al. [47] reanalyzed these data and confirmed the low dust content of MRG-M0138.

The Na- and dust-based $f_{\rm gas}$ measurements are thus significantly different. Both approaches carry substantial uncertainties. The Na I D doublet becomes optically thick at relatively low column densities [109], and once the line is saturated, increasing the column density no longer increases the absorption depth, which is then mainly set by the covering fraction [50, 78, 101, 21]. In addition, in realistic ISM conditions, Na I D absorption originates from multiple narrow velocity components that may be unresolved [106, 145, 146]. When blended, these components can contain saturated substructure that appear as a shallower, broader feature, leading to underestimated column densities. This bias is expected to be more severe in systems with large gas velocity dispersions, like MRG-M0138. Finally, absorption measurements cannot detect any gas within highly obscured clouds. Although the galaxy is dust-poor, Na I requires dust shielding to survive and so may exist in small, dusty clumps. For these reasons, gas masses derived from Na I D absorption should be regarded as lower limits.

On the other hand, gas mass estimates derived from the dust continuum are highly sensitive to assumptions about the dust temperature ( $T_{\rm dust}$ ) and the gas-to-dust ratio ( $\delta_{\rm GDR}$ ). Reported values of $T_{\rm dust}$ span a broad range [117], with several studies finding temperatures significantly lower than the commonly adopted value of 25 K [46, 72, 24]. In addition, the relation between gas and dust mass in quiescent galaxies remains poorly constrained, with observational estimates spanning a wide range of $\delta_{\rm GDR}\approx 40-1200$ [148, 82, 71, 121]. Reconciling the Na- and dust-based $f_{\rm gas}$ estimates by varying $T_{\rm dust}$ or $\delta_{\rm GDR}$ alone would require extreme values ( $T_{\rm dust}\gtrsim 100$ K or $\delta_{\rm GDR}\lesssim 15$ ), which are unlikely for a quiescent galaxy [148, 71]. This instead suggests that the discrepancy arises at least in part from systematic uncertainties in the Na-based estimates.

In summary, the available tracers consistently point to an extremely low gas fraction in MRG-M0138, although the exact value remains uncertain due to systematic limitations inherent to Na I D absorption and dust continuum measurements. Na I D is a sensitive tracer of neutral gas and is effective at mapping its spatial distribution and kinematics. Our comparison of gas mass tracers suggests that Na-based masses are likely lower limits.

## V Star-Formation Histories

Motivated by signs that the some gas in MRG-M0138 may have been recently accreted, in this section we investigate the galaxy’s star-formation history (SFH) using Prospector, a Bayesian Spectral Energy Distribution (SED) fitting code [56, 67].

### V.1 Modeling the Galaxy SED

Our Prospector fits employed the Flexible Stellar Population Synthesis (FSPS; Conroy et al. 27, Conroy and Gunn 28) models based on the MESA Isochrones and Stellar Tracks (MIST; Dotter 36, Choi et al. 23), the MILES spectral library [41], and a Kroupa IMF [62]. The SED model includes 18 free parameters describing the contributions of stars, gas, and dust. The stellar component is characterized by the redshift, stellar mass formed, stellar velocity dispersion, metallicity (with abundance ratios assumed to be solar), and a SFH.

*Figure 10: Non-parametric SFHs are shown for four distinct spatial regions within MRG-M0138. In each panel, the dark and light shaded regions indicate the 1 $\sigma$ and 2 $\sigma$ posterior intervals, respectively. The colored curves denotes the posterior medians, while the dashed black lines shows the maximum a posteriori (MAP) SFH.*

We adopted a non-parametric approach [66, 65], dividing the SFH into discrete time bins without imposing any predetermined functional form. While this method increases the number of free parameters in the fit, it offers greater flexibility in capturing the true diversity of SFHs. We adopted 12 age bins: two narrow bins at young ages ( $0-75$ Myr and $75-150$ Myr), followed by five linearly spaced bins between 300 Myr and 1 Gyr to better resolve recent and intermediate star formation. At older ages, we used logarithmically spaced bins extending up to $97\%$ of the age of the universe at the galaxy’s redshift.

Prospector fits ratios of the star formation rates (SFRs) in adjacent time bins ( $\Delta\log\text{SFR}$ ). A Student-t “continuity” prior is applied to each of these ratios to encourage smooth transitions between bins while allowing for sharp changes where necessary. We used the parameters $\sigma=0.3$ and $\nu=2.0$ following Leja et al. [65]. To assess the robustness of our inferred SFHs, we additionally tested a “bursty” prior, which is a modified version of the continuity prior with $\sigma=1.0$ . This prior does not explicitly favor sharp transitions but permits more flexible changes in star formation activity compared to the baseline continuity prior [128, 129]. The results do not change much with the change in prior.

Dust attenuation was modeled using a single-component [16] attenuation curve applied uniformly to all stars. Therefore, only the dust parameter describing attenuation of the older stellar light is included, while the parameter for additional attenuation of young stars is fixed to zero. This is appropriate for MRG-M0138, which is an old, quiescent system with no significant young stellar population. We also experimented with dust attenuation curves that allow a variable UV slope [61], but we found this did not affect our inferred SFHs. Additionally, Prospector can model emission lines using Gaussian profiles and analytically marginalizing their amplitudes, assuming a shared velocity offset and velocity dispersion for all lines that we considered: H $\alpha$ , H $\beta$ , H $\gamma$ , H $\delta$ , [O II] $\lambda\lambda$ 3727, 3730, [O III] $\lambda\lambda$ 4960, 5008, [N II] $\lambda\lambda$ 6550, 6585, and [S II] $\lambda\lambda$ 6718, 6733. We also included a “jitter” parameter that scales the reported spectroscopic flux uncertainties [56]. In practice, the inferred jitter values are generally close to unity, as expected given that the uncertainties were already rescaled based on our pPXF fits. Although robust likelihood methods with mixture models [56] can mitigate sensitivity to outlier spectral pixels, we did not employ such an approach because outliers were already removed at the spaxel level prior to the Prospector analysis.

We simultaneously fit the NIRSpec spectra and matched seven-band photometry in several spatial bins described below. We fit the spectra over the rest-frame wavelength range 4000–6700 Å following Park et al. [90]. This range covers many age-sensitive spectral features such as Balmer absorption lines. We used a polynomial order of 6 to modulate the continuum of the spectrum. We masked the Na I D and Ca II K $\&$ H absorption lines, which are affected by gas absorption, as well as the Mg I b feature, which is strongly affected by $\alpha$ enhancement. To explore the posterior distribution, we use the Dynesty dynamic nested sampling algorithm [119].

### V.2 Spatially Resolved Star Formation Histories

To investigate how the SFH varies across the galaxy, we measured the SFH in a series of four spatial bins. These bins were defined to probe distinct structural components of the galaxy: the nucleus (the region within $R_{\rm e,bulge}/4$ ), bulge (within $R_{\rm e,bulge}$ ), inner disk (within $R_{\rm e,disk}$ ), and outer disk (within $2R_{\rm e,disk}$ ).55 5 Each region is defined as elliptical aperture with an axial ratio appropriate to the bulge or disk [87]. Each bin excludes the regions interior to it, and thus the bins are non-overlapping and the spectrophotometric data are independent. Figure 9 presents the spectroscopic and photometric data for the nucleus spatial bin of MRG-M0138, along with the corresponding Prospector fit.

Figure 10 shows that the resulting SFHs are quite uniform across the galaxy. Moreover, the bulk of MRG-M0138 is quite ancient, with most of the star-formation occurring at lookback times $>2.5$ Gyr that correspond to $z\gtrsim 6$ . Approximately 500 Myr ago, we see evidence of a rejuvenation of star formation in every spatial bin. The fraction of the stellar mass formed in this event is small, ranging from about $2\%-9\%$ across the bins. We found that switching from the continuity prior to the bursty prior did not appreciably alter the resulting SFHs, nor did modifying the age bin structure. Therefore the qualitative features appear robust.

We quantify the significance of recent star formation enhancements using the posterior distribution of $\rm\Delta SFR_{burst}$ , a metric defined to capture the strength of the burst. Specifically, $\rm\Delta SFR_{burst}$ is defined as the difference between the SFR at the peak of the secondary burst and the SFR at a lookback time of $\sim 1~\rm Gyr$ . The statistical significance is evaluated from the posterior probability that $\rm\Delta SFR_{burst}>0$ . This yields evidence of rejuvenation across different regions, with a significance of $\rm 2.7\sigma,~6.9\sigma,~7.1\sigma~and~1.7\sigma$ in the nucleus, bulge, inner disk, and outer disk, respectively.

Akhshik et al. [1] analyzed the spatially resolved SFH of MRG-M0138 based on HST grism spectroscopy. The early SFR peak that we observe is consistent with their findings. Although their analysis shows a more gradual decline in SFR and does not exhibit a secondary peak, these differences may arise from variations in methodology (e.g., the adopted SFH priors) as well as from the data itself, given that the JWST observations provide a broader wavelength coverage and much higher spectral resolution.

Since rejuvenation of quiescent galaxies is thought to be triggered by gas accretion [153, 57, 76], these SFHs provide additional evidence for gas accretion and constraints on its timing. An alternative scenario is that these $\rm\sim 500~Myr$ -old stars formed in a younger satellite that was accreted through a minor merger. A dry merger contributing a pre-existing stellar population could , in principle, explain the secondary “burst” that we see in the SFH. However, as we will discuss in Section VII, the kinematics and distribution of the gas, together with the timing of the rejuvenation episode, favor a scenario in which externally acquired gas fueled renewed in situ star formation.

## VI The Environment of MRG-M0138

Studies of $z\gtrsim 1$ quiescent and post-starburst galaxies in which CO was detected have frequently found evidence for interactions, mergers, or rejuvenation episodes [8, 124, 154]. In this context, and motivated by evidence of recent external gas accretion in MRG–M0138, we searched for nearby galaxies that could have recently interacted with it. The SFH derived from the integrated spectrophotometric data of MRG-M0138 indicates that approximately $\sim 10^{10}~\rm M_{\odot}~(\sim 5\%~of~M_{\star}$ ; Section II) of mass was formed during the rejuvenation episode $\rm\sim 500~Myrs$ ago. If this episode is attributed to an interaction or merger, the other galaxy would need to have contributed at least this mass of gas and/or stars. Hence, we do not expect the rejuvenation to be associated with a low-mass ( $\rm\lesssim 10^{9}~M_{\odot}$ ) companion. Our search revealed two compelling candidate companions (Figure 11).

*Figure 11: Two galaxies possibly associated with MRG-M0138 are identified in a JWST/NIRCam image through the F150W, F356W, and F444W filters, displayed with a logarithmic stretch. Galaxy 1: A multiply imaged galaxy to the north with a tentative spectroscopic redshift and a projected separation from MRG-M0138 of 77 kpc in the source plane [127]. Galaxy 2: A dusty, extremely red galaxy to the west with a photometric redshift consistent with MRG-M0138 and a projected separation of 64 kpc.*

The first candidate (labelled 1 in Figure 11), was identified in Suyu et al. [127] as the “silver lensed system.” It consists of an arc that Suyu et al. [127] identified as being formed by two blended background sources that are strongly lensed. They reported a likely spectroscopic redshift of $z_{\rm silver}=1.945$ , consistent with the redshift of MRG-M0138 at $z=1.948$ [87]. The projected separation between this source and MRG-M0138 is 77 kpc in the source plane. Because the photometry is blended and it is not entirely clear that there are two separate sources, we measured aperture photometry over the whole arc (see Figure 11) and used Prospector to model the data. The same set of parameters and age bins as for MRG-M0138 were adopted, but with the redshift fixed to that of MRG-M0138. Since our photometry combines three merging images, we use the sum of the magnifications $\mu\approx 32$ from the GLAFIC lens model discussed by Suyu et al. [127].66 6 We used this lens model because it was one of two in the set of seven lens models discussed by Suyu et al. [127] to use the silver system as a constraint. The best-fit model yields $A_{V}=0.24$ , a demagnified stellar mass of $\rm M_{*}=9\times 10^{9}~\rm M_{\odot}$ , and a star-formation rate in the most recent age bin of $\rm{SFR}\approx 0.8~\rm M_{\odot}~{yr}^{-1}$ , indicating that this galaxy has a moderate mass, a low SFR, and low dust attenuation.

We searched for additional companions using photometric redshift estimates generated by applying the EAZY code [15] to our 7-band HST and JWST photometry. We considered sources within $40^{\prime\prime}$ of the cluster center with a photometic redshift estimate $|z_{\rm phot}-1.95|<0.25$ . We further restricted to galaxies with an estimated stellar mass $\rm M_{*}>10^{10}$ M⊙ to reduce contamination by the large population of low-mass galaxies, most of which will be in the foreground or background, and to focus on galaxies massive enough to have triggered the observed rejuvenation.

This search identified one additional source (labeled 2 in Figure 11), an extremely red galaxy located west of the cluster core. Its estimated photometric redshift $z_{\rm phot}=1.82\pm 0.18$ is consistent with MRG-M0138, it lies at a projected separation of 64 kpc in the source plane, and its magnification is $\mu=4.5^{+1.3}_{-0.7}$ according to the Ertl et al. [39] lens model. We modeled the data using Prospector, adopting the same configuration as for target 1. The best-fit model indicates a massive ( $\rm M_{*}=5\times 10^{10}~M_{\odot}$ , approximately one-quarter that of MRG–M0138) and dusty ( $A_{\rm V}=1.9$ ) galaxy. The SFR in the most recent bin is relatively low ( $\approx 10~{\rm M_{\odot}~yr}^{-1}$ ), but we regard this as uncertain given the high attenuation.

Although secure spectroscopic redshifts are needed to make a unambiguous connection, these galaxies are likely associated with MRG-M0138. Given the surface density of galaxies matching the same $z_{\rm phot}$ and $\rm M_{*}$ criteria in the COSMOS-Web catalog [115], we would expect only 0.03 foreground or background contaminants within 77 kpc of MRG-M0138. Although the galaxies are probably not strongly interacting with MRG-M0138 at the observed epoch, they are close enough to have interacted strongly in the past, in particular 500 Myr ago when then rejuvenation event occurred. These considerations suggest that we have found galaxies capable of having acted as a gas donor through past tidal interactions.

## VII Discussion

We present high-resolution maps of the gas and dust in a quiescent galaxy at $z=1.95$ , providing a detailed view of its cold ISM. Previous ALMA studies have shown that quiescent galaxies at these redshifts are typically dust-poor and, by implication, gas-poor [13, 150, 149, e.g.,], although the relationship between gas and dust mass is not necessarily tight [82, 71, 121]. MRG-M0138 is notable in this context, as it was one of only two quiescent galaxies detected at 1.3 mm in the Whitaker et al. [149] sample and was inferred to have a low gas fraction, as confirmed by Gobat et al. [47]. However, prior observations lacked the spatial resolution required to resolve the dust distribution, and dust continuum observations do not enable kinematic measures.

Spatially resolved maps of the ISM provide critical insight into the origin of the remaining gas and dust in quiescent systems. In particular, they allow us to assess whether this gas represents residual ISM that survived quenching, stellar mass loss from evolved populations, or gas accreted externally. Distinguishing among these scenarios has direct implications for the completeness and long-term maintenance of quenching. It is also closely connected to the fueling of AGN feedback, which is increasingly thought to be common in high-redshift quiescent galaxies and potentially central to both the quenching process and the suppression of subsequent star formation [32, 108, 118, 40, 7, 133].

### VII.1 Gas Kinematics

In MRG-M0138, we detect gas absorption from the nuclear regions to the outermost radii that we probe in the disk. The gas is kinematically aligned with the stars, yet it rotates more slowly (Figures 7 and 8). Slower gas rotation relative to the circular velocity is often interpreted as the result of turbulent pressure support, which acts as a perturbation to the rotational speed in a kinematically cold disk [33, e.g.,]. Turbulence could be very important in MRG-M0138, since the observed gas velocity dispersions are extremely large, $\sigma_{\rm gas}\gtrsim 200$ km s-1 in all spatial bins and reaching $\approx 400$ km s-1 or higher (Figure 6). However, the magnitude of any rotational lag is difficult to quantify, as it depends on the uncertain [Na/Fe]* abundance (Figure 8), and the gas velocity dispersion is also challenging to measure (Section III.5).

Moreover, the observed line width $\sigma_{\rm gas}$ is likely to be strongly affected by rotational broadening, a consequence of projection through a highly inclined galaxy, PSF convolution, and spatial binning. In the fiducial stellar dynamical model of Newman et al. [87], when these effects are taken into account, the smallest stellar velocity dispersion expected to be measured is $\sigma_{*}=189$ km s-1, which is much higher than the intrinsic stellar velocity dispersion of about 70 km s-1 in the disk-dominated region. All of these effects make it difficult to accurately measure the gas turbulence and quantitatively interpret the rotation lag. The most robust conclusion is that the rotation fields of the gas and stars are kinematically aligned.

This corotation of the gas and stars disfavors the presence of large-scale gas outflows in MRG-M0138, as have been reported in many massive galaxies at $z\gtrsim 2$ [37, 9, 34, 152, 135, 69]. We found that the systemic velocity of the gas may be slightly blueshifted with respect to the stars, but the magnitude of any such offset is comparable to the systematic uncertainties (Section III.5). A handful of spatial bins show gas that may be blueshifted relative to the local stellar velocity, with differences of up to $\sim\rm 260~km~s^{-1}$ (Figure 8, left panel), but the gas kinematics are uncertain in these bins: they fail our significance threshold under the sodium-enhanced scenario, [Na/Fe]* = +0.6. We therefore do not interpret these as outflows. We also see no sign of coherent inflows, including in the dust lane, which would be detectable as regions with $V_{\rm gas}>V_{\rm stars}$ in Figure 8. The gas may be slowly infalling, but its kinematics are dominated by disk motion.

### VII.2 Spatial Distribution of Gas and Dust

Spatially, the gas in MRG-M0138 does not appear to be in a equilibrium configuration, due to the presence of a prominent one-sided dust lane, a trailing wedge-shaped structure in the outer disk, and an off-nuclear concentration of gas and dust. This argues against stellar mass loss as the dominant origin of the gas, since material shed by stars would be expected to follow the stellar spatial distribution more closely. While the stars must have released substantial amounts of gas and dust since quenching, most of this material is likely heated and thus not observable in a cold phase, as long established for local early-type galaxies [138]. Disturbed gas morphologies and dust features in local early-type galaxies are commonly interpreted as signatures of recent accretion or merger events [103, 112, 60, 104].

Secondary episodes of star formation, or rejuvenation, are also often attributed to mergers or gas accretion [76, 57, 91, 142]. The star formation histories that we inferred with Prospector reveal a minor, galaxy-wide rejuvenation episode approximately 500 Myr ago (Figure 10), providing a plausible timing for at least one gas accretion event. The time since accretion must be long enough for the gas to have been torqued by the stellar disk into corotation, as we observe. This timescale has been explored in simulations by van de Voort et al. [137]. Once the gas supply is largely shut off, they find that kinematic settling occurs on a timescale of roughly $6t_{\rm dyn}$ , and potentially twice as long to reach complete alignment. Defining the dynamical time as $t_{\rm dyn}=2\pi R/v_{\rm circ}$ , we estimate $t_{\rm dyn}\rm\approx 50~Myr$ in the outer spatial bins. This implies a kinematic settling timescale of $\sim 300-600$ Myr, strikingly close to the epoch of minor rejuvenation. This suggests that the gas has had enough time to kinematically settle. If the gas arrived on a nearly corotating orbit, still less time may have been required.

The spatial distribution of the gas may take longer to reach equilibrium. If the gas in MRG-M0138 was accreted over an extended period, for instance, through the slow fallback of tidal gas ejected during a merger or interaction, the continued infall of material could delay relaxation to an equilibrium configuration [137, 35]. Indeed, we identify two galaxies that may have interacted with MRG-M0138 (Section VI). The nearer galaxy is remarkably red, dusty, and presumably gas-rich. While the projected separation may not support a strong ongoing interaction, the galaxies may have been closer when the accretion occurred $\sim 500$ Myr ago. Although further observations and simulations are needed to explore this scenario in detail, interactions between these galaxies and MRG-M0138 are certainly a plausible origin of the accreted gas. As highlighted by Whitaker et al. [147], globular cluster systems serve as an independent probe of merger and accretion histories, and a similar analysis is currently underway for MRG-M0138 (Matthews et al., in prep).

Despite the overall disturbed morphology of the gas and dust, one of its main components is a remarkably clear dust lane that is readily visible in the NIRCam imaging (Figure 7A). Studies of local ETGs show that the net dust depletion time can extend to a $\sim$ Gyr [80], implying that dust acquired $\sim 500$ Myr ago could plausibly still be observable. More surprising would be for the dust to have persisted in this coherent, linear configuration for roughly ten dynamical times [35]. Although the dust lane appears sharply defined in the image, the $N_{\rm Na~I}$ and color maps (Figure 7, panel D-F) are more sensitive to lower densities. Together with the velocity field, these show that the dust lane is the leading edge of an extended wedge of gas and dust in the outer disk, suggesting that it may be a dynamical structure formed by interactions between accreted gas and pre-existing ISM. Alternatively, gas accretion may be episodic, and the material in the dust lane could have been acquired more recently than the rejuvenation event.

### VII.3 Implications for Feedback and Quenching

Our results reinforce the interpretation of Whitaker et al. [149] that quenching at high redshifts is highly effective at removing or heating the interstellar medium. In particular, our analysis suggests that at least one of the dust detections in that work arises from material accreted after quenching, rather than from residual gas left over from the star-forming phase. Moreover, while the decline of the gas or dust reservoirs of quenched galaxies is often modeled as a smooth gas consumption history [46, e.g.,], MRG-M0138 is a reminder that the external accretion of gas can complicate this picture. Its little remaining gas is probably not related to the main quenching event.

The gas may, however, be related to the maintenance of quiescence. The off-nuclear clump of gas and dust is located extremely close to the galaxy center, at a projected distance of only $\approx 0.01^{\prime\prime}\approx 90$ pc. Given its proximity, this material could soon feed the $\rm 6\times 10^{9}~M_{\odot}$ supermassive black hole at the center of MRG-M0138 [87], which is currently inactive. Such accretion could plausibly trigger an episode of black hole feedback. Low-luminosity AGN are common in local early-type galaxies, often referred to as “red geysers” [22, 97, 54, 45], where episodic feedback events may provide sufficient energy to prevent gas cooling and star formation. In the prototype red geyser system, Akira [22], the gas fueling the central black hole appears to have been supplied via a tidal interaction. Evidence for episodic AGN feedback in high-redshift quiescent galaxies has also been discussed by Taylor et al. [131], who propose that outflows may later fall back as inflows if the gas cannot escape completely, thereby reigniting AGN activity on timescales of $\sim$ 40 Myr.

These neutral gas outflows appear to be more common and more powerful in galaxies that were quenched within the last $\sim 1$ Gyr [90, 132, 126, 131]. Our SFH analysis indicates that the main quenching event in MRG–M0138 occurred $\gtrsim 2.5$ Gyr ago at $z\gtrsim 6$ (Figure 10), placing it among the earliest galaxies to quench. The old age of MRG-M0138 could explain its lack of outflows. Furthermore, these population studies imply that the gas in MRG-M0138 has probably not been continually recycled since the main quenching period, and they therefore support our interpretation that the gas was acquired afterward.

### VII.4 The Weak Calcium Absorption in MRG-M0138

While Na I gas absorption is widespread across MRG-M0138, we detect much weaker Ca II H and K absorption only through stacking (Section III.4). We estimate a lower column density of Ca II, with $\log(N_{\rm Na~I}/N_{\rm Ca~II})=0.19^{+0.22}_{-0.32}$ . This is near the upper limit of the range $-0.8\lesssim\log(N_{\rm Na~I}/N_{\rm Ca~II})\lesssim 0.3$ recently observed in a sample of $z\sim 2$ galaxies, both quiescent and star-forming [69]. Therefore the much weaker Ca II H $\&$ K absorption compared to Na I D is not highly unusual.

The abundance of calcium in interstellar gas is highly sensitive to the ionization state and dust depletion, whereas sodium is comparatively less affected [51, 11, 107, 144, 58, 139]. Specifically, cold ( $T\sim 30$ K), dense ( $n_{H}\geq 10^{3}~{\rm cm}^{-3}$ ) diffuse molecular clouds, where most of the gas-phase calcium is depleted onto grains, typically exhibit Na I/Ca II $\geq 100$ , whereas values two or more orders of magnitude lower are characteristic of warmer ( $T\sim 10^{3}$ K), lower-density environments where much of the calcium remains in the gas phase [52, 11, 31]. In addition, shocks can liberate calcium from grain surfaces [96, 116, 30, 136, 111]. The relatively high $N_{\rm Na~I}/N_{\rm Ca~II}$ that we measure in MRG-M0138 compared to other quiescent galaxies at similar redshift [69] suggests cooler conditions. Qualitatively, the old stellar population (Figure 10) and quiescent black hole [87] in MRG-M0138 are consistent with a weaker far-ultraviolet radiation field and less photoelectric heating. Moreover, the gas absorption in about half of the Liboni et al. [69] galaxies is blueshifted, indicating that it is produced in an outflow where the physical conditions may be more favorable for dust grain destruction (hence less Ca II depletion).

## VIII Conclusions and Summary

We present the first highly resolved picture of gas and dust in a $z\sim 2$ quiescent galaxy. We analyzed JWST/NIRSpec IFU observations of the remarkable lensed galaxy MRG-M0138, complemented by HST and JWST/NIRCam imaging in seven filters. The high magnification of this galaxy ( $\mu\sim 29$ at center) enables us to extract high-quality spectra in 219 spatial bins. We traced the spatial distribution and kinematics of the neutral gas using Na I D absorption, as well as the dust distribution by mapping the attenuation. Our main results are summarized below.

- • We detected Na I D absorption (beyond the stellar contribution) tracing neutral gas in most spatial bins across a wide range of plausible stellar [Na/Fe]* values (Figure 4). In contrast, Ca II H and K absorption is much weaker and only detectable in stacked spectra.

- • The Na I D absorption traces a smooth velocity field with clear rotation that is aligned with the stellar velocity field but slower, likely due to turbulent pressure support. We find no evidence for large-scale inflows or outflows like those seen in some high-redshift quiescent galaxies, possibly reflecting the galaxy’s old stellar population and early quenching.

- • The gas and dust show a highly inhomogeneous distribution, including a one-sided radial dust lane, a trailing wedge of clumpy material in the disk, and a clump near but offset from the nucleus (Figure 7). This disturbed morphology favors an external accretion origin for most or all of the gas and dust, rather than residual material from quenching or stellar mass loss.

- • Using Prospector, we modeled the spatially resolved SFH of MRG–M0138, finding rapid quenching $\sim 2.5$ Gyr ago followed by $\sim 2$ Gyr of quiescence. A minor rejuvenation episode $\sim 500$ Myr ago is detected, possibly triggered by external gas accretion. This timescale matches that required for accreted gas to be torqued into corotation with the stellar disk.

- • We identified two galaxies at projected separations of 61–77 kpc from MRG–M0138, one with a tentative spectroscopic redshift and one with a consistent photometric redshift, making them plausible sources of tidally acquired gas.

- • MRG–M0138 was one of only two $z\sim 2$ quiescent galaxies detected in ALMA dust continuum emission by Whitaker et al. [149]. Our spatially resolved analysis suggests that this gas is not a remnant of the early quenching phase, but instead was likely accreted recently from a nearby companion. This reinforces the conclusion by Whitaker et al. [149] that quenching in massive high-redshift galaxies efficiently consumed or removed gas.

- • The off-nuclear gas clump lies $\sim 0.1$ arcsec ( $\approx 90$ pc) from the central SMBH, making it a plausible fuel source for future AGN feedback. This highlights a pathway in which external gas accretion triggers AGN activity. Recurrent feedback may help maintain quiescence in MRG–M0138, akin to local “red geysers,” and AGN feedback seeded by mergers or accretion may similarly power some of the winds seen in recently quenched $z\sim 2$ galaxies.

A comprehensive analysis of the full INQUEST-JWST sample is currently underway. By extending the approaches developed in this study to a larger sample of lensed, quiescent galaxies, we will assess the incidence and properties of inflows and outflows, as well as the origin of any residual interstellar gas. Ultimately we aim to test whether hidden gas accretion and feedback cycles represent a ubiquitous mechanism for maintaining quiescence at high redshift.

## Abstract

We analyze JWST/NIRSpec IFU spectroscopy of MRG-M0150, a gravitationally lensed, massive quiescent galaxy at $z=2.6$ from the INQUEST-JWST survey. Thanks to the combination of lensing magnification with JWST’s angular resolution, we are able to build spatially resolved maps of the ionized gas spatial distribution, kinematics, and ionization properties in this system. We detect ionized gas emission throughout the galaxy: the lack of residual star formation inferred from line-ratio diagnostic diagrams, together with the decoupling between the gas and stellar kinematics, suggest that the ionized gas is in a wind. We use the 3D gas kinematics modeling code MOKA3D to constrain the geometry and physical properties of the ionized gas wind. We find that the observations are consistent with a biconical wind driven by the low-luminosity AGN at the center of the galaxy, which is detected in X-rays. The wind reaches high velocities of $\approx 1000-1400$ km s-1, implying that part of the gas may escape the halo. The ionized gas mass outflow rate, $(0.6\pm 0.2)$ ${\rm M}_{\odot}$ yr-1, is modest but exceeds the upper limit on the residual star formation rate, and it is likely that the wind is multiphase and carries more mass. We show that typical unresolved observations would not detect the wind, suggesting that the incidence of such outflows may be higher than previously recognized. Simple geometric arguments show that the observed outflow must have been launched $\approx 0.45$ Myr ago from the time of observation. This evidence suggests that low-level AGN activity is an important mechanism for maintaining quiescence in massive galaxies at cosmic noon, potentially over cosmological timescales.

#### Key Words.

## 1 Introduction

The physical processes responsible for the quenching of star-formation in massive galaxies remain one of the key open problems in galaxy formation and evolution. Numerous mechanisms have been proposed to explain the quenching of massive galaxies, including active galactic nuclei (AGN), stellar feedback, and virial shock heating (see Whitaker and Bezanson, 2026, for a recent review), but no single mechanism seems to be universally applicable. Semi-analytical models and cosmological hydrodynamical simulations typically invoke AGN feedback as a mechanism capable of quenching massive galaxies. Feedback from the AGN can drive galaxy-scale outflows in multiple gas phases, quenching the galaxy both by expelling gas from the system and by heating the circumgalactic medium, thereby preventing the cooling and accretion of gas that could otherwise fuel subsequent star formation (Di Matteo et al., 2005; Hopkins et al., 2006; Bower et al., 2006; Somerville et al., 2008; Davé et al., 2019, e.g.). However, direct observational evidence linking AGN feedback to the quenching of star formation remains elusive. At cosmic noon ( $z\sim 2-3$ ), a significant fraction of massive galaxies stopped forming new stars (Muzzin et al., 2013; Straatman et al., 2014; Tomczak et al., 2014; Weaver et al., 2023, e.g.). Observing recently quenched systems at this epoch is crucial for investigating the main mechanisms responsible for quenching star formation in the most massive galaxies.

*Figure 1: Left: Median signal-to-noise ratio along the wavelength axis of the IFU data cube. Overplotted in white are the boundaries of the Voronoi bins analyzed. Right: One example spectrum extracted from the central spaxel (blue) with the pPXF stellar continuum fit overlaid in red.*

Galaxy-scale gas outflows have been extensively studied at $z\sim 1-3$ through large galaxy surveys. It has been found that outflows are ubiquitous in massive star-forming galaxies at cosmic noon (Steidel et al., 2010; Weiner et al., 2009; Förster Schreiber et al., 2019) and in those hosting the most luminous AGN (Cano-Díaz et al., 2012; Cresci et al., 2015a; Kakkad et al., 2016; Davies et al., 2020b), where they are expected to be powerful enough to be able to suppress star formation. However, the study of gas outflows and nuclear activity in the first quiescent galaxies at high redshift is challenging from the ground, relying either on deep exposures of individual galaxies (Kriek et al., 2024; Belli et al., 2017, e.g.) or stacked spectra (Belli et al., 2019, e.g.).

The launch of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has opened a new window on the high-redshift Universe, revealing an abundant population of massive quiescent galaxies already in place at $z>2$ (Carnall et al., 2023a; Weibel et al., 2025; Nanayakkara et al., 2024; de Graaff et al., 2025). Early JWST spectra of individual galaxies have revealed the presence of AGN activity in these systems (Carnall et al., 2023b; Belli et al., 2024; D’Eugenio et al., 2024; Wu, 2025) and subsequent studies with larger samples have confirmed a high AGN incidence in massive quiescent galaxies at $z>2$ (Bugiani et al., 2025; Skarbinski et al., 2026). These AGN, for the most part, have been classified as low-luminosity AGN (LL-AGN), based on their faint inferred bolometric luminosities and the lack of more overt tracers of powerful AGN activity such as X-rays detection or IR excess (Almaini et al., 2025; Hewitt et al., 2026).

At the same time, JWST observations have revealed a widespread presence of gas outflows in massive quiescent galaxies at high redshift, detected both in the neutral and ionized phases (Davies et al., 2024; Taylor et al., 2026; Valentino et al., 2025; Sapori et al., 2026; Sun et al., 2026). These outflows can be remarkably powerful, often carrying large amounts of cold gas. In particular, observations of neutral-phase outflows in $z>2$ galaxies through the Na D absorption line have shown that powerful winds are prevalent among massive galaxies at cosmic noon and may represent the dominant pathway for quenching at this epoch (Davies et al., 2024; Sapori et al., 2026). In some systems, the inferred neutral-phase mass outflow rates exceed the current star-formation rates by more than an order of magnitude, suggesting that efficient removal of cold gas may contribute directly to the rapid quenching observed in these galaxies (Belli et al., 2024; D’Eugenio et al., 2024).

However, the origin of these galactic winds and their connection to star-formation quenching remain unclear, as the low-level AGN activity observed in many massive systems struggles to explain the high energy and momentum rates characterizing the observed outflows. While some studies attribute the origin of the observed winds to ongoing LL-AGN activity (Belli et al., 2024; Wu, 2025; Bugiani et al., 2025, e.g.), others interpret them as relics of past starburst episodes or previous periods of more powerful black hole activity, with the central AGN having since faded into a low-accretion state (Valentino et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026; Taylor et al., 2026). Distinguishing between these scenarios is therefore crucial for establishing whether the outflows observed in massive quiescent galaxies represent ongoing AGN feedback or the remnants of the events that originally quenched the galaxy.

With only a few exceptions (Gangula et al., 2026; D’Eugenio et al., 2024), most studies rely on spatially unresolved data and therefore are not able to directly constrain the geometry, kinematics, and timescales of the outflows. While the ionized phase may represent a small contribution to the total outflowing mass, as observed in high- $z$ quiescent galaxies (Belli et al., 2024) and predicted by simulations of galactic winds (Kim et al., 2020), it is the best suited to measuring these properties. Ionized gas can be detected directly in emission without requiring a bright background continuum. Its emission traces the full spatial extent of the wind, and, provided that it can be spatially resolved, yields detailed information about the kinematics and 3D structure of the outflow. This can reduce some of the uncertainties associated with assumptions about the geometry and kinematics when deriving mass outflow rates and energetics. Moreover, reconstructing the extent, geometry, and velocity of the winds provides a way to constrain their characteristic timescales, which can be used to distinguish between winds powered by ongoing AGN activity and fossil outflows launched by a past quasar or starburst event. Resolved observations of the ionized phase can therefore offer a unique view on the connection between AGN activity, galactic outflows, and the maintenance of quiescence in massive galaxies at high redshift.

In this work, we investigate ionized gas emission in MRG-M0150, a strongly-lensed, massive quiescent galaxy at $z=2.64$ (Newman et al., 2015) using spatially resolved observations obtained by JWST/NIRSpec in IFU mode. We make use of the combined sensitivity of JWST and gravitational lensing magnification to characterize the geometry, velocity, and energetics of the ionized gas outflow observed in this system, and use it to investigate the connection between the outflow and the quenching of star-formation in this galaxy. In Section 2, we present the observations used in this paper. In Section 3, we describe the emission-line fitting and discuss the resulting maps and resolved emission-line diagnostics, as well as the AGN activity and residual star formation. In Section 4, we construct a 3D kinematic model of the observed ionized gas outflow and derive its main properties. In Section 5, we perform SED fitting of the integrated light from the galaxy to reconstruct its star-formation history (SFH). We discuss our results in Section 6 and summarize our main conclusions in Section 7. Throughout this paper, we assume the WMAP9 cosmology (Hinshaw et al., 2013) and a Chabrier (2003) initial mass function.

## 2 Target and observations

MRG-M0150 is a massive quiescent galaxy at $z=2.64$ , multiply imaged by the galaxy cluster MACS J0150.3 $-$ 1005 at $z=0.365$ (Newman et al., 2015). A JWST/NIRCam image of the cluster, with the multiple images of our target labeled, can be found in Fig. 11 in Appendix A. The galaxy has a stellar mass of $\log(M/M_{\odot})=11.30\pm 0.04$ – derived by the integrated SED fitting, see Sect. 5 – and is classified as a “fast rotator,” exhibiting a rotationally supported stellar disk (Newman et al., 2018a; Newman et al., 2018b). It has a circularized half-light radius of $R_{e}\sim 0.2$ arcsec (corresponding to 1.6 kpc on the source plane), as found by the lens modeling (Appendix A). Dynamical models indicate that the inclination of the stellar disk is $\sim 30^{\circ}$ (Newman et al., 2018b).11 1 These models were constrained by ground-based slit spectra. Dynamical modeling of the JWST IFU data indicates a similar inclination of $\sim 40^{\circ}$ (Newman et al., in prep.).

The target belongs to the INQUEST-JWST galaxy sample, which includes 5 gravitationally lensed, massive and quiescent galaxies at redshift $z=2.1-2.6$ . Data used in this paper comes from the Cycle 3 JWST GO-4903 observational program. The program observed one image of MRG-M0150, labeled Image 1 in the cluster image visible in Fig.11, using the JWST/NIRSpec IFU with the G140M/F100LP and G235M/F170LP grating/filter pairs. Exposure times were 4.4 hours for each setting. Additionally, the same program acquired NIRCam imaging with total exposure times of 20-30 minutes in the F115W, F200W, F277W and F444W filters. We also make use of archival imaging data from the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) through the F814W filter (Newman et al., 2015) for the full SED fitting (Sect.6.4).

The NIRSpec data cubes were reduced using the JWST Science Data Processing system version 2025_3a and the JWST Science Calibration Pipeline version 2.0.0. Spectral “wiggles” – artifacts affecting NIRSpec data due to undersampling of the PSF – were mitigated using the adaptive trace model step in the pipeline. We detected some residual wiggles, which we modeled and removed using the procedure described in Newman et al. (2026). We created output data cubes with a $0.1^{\prime\prime}$ spaxel scale for the G140M and G235M observations. The fluxes and variances are logarithmically rebinned onto a wavelength grid with 132 km s-1 per pixel and shifted to the systemic rest frame ( $z_{\rm sys}=2.6355$ ). Then they are combined by splicing them together at $\lambda_{rest}=0.505\>\mu$ m. Noise spectra coming out of the pipeline are rescaled based on residuals to the stellar continuum model fits (Sect. 3.1). The resulting data cube is spatially binned to a signal-to-noise target of 40 using the vorbin algorithm (Cappellari and Copin, 2012; Cappellari and Copin, 2003). A visualization of the resulting Voronoi bins can be seen in the left panel of Figure 1. We also measure PSF-matched photometry in each spatial bin for every photometric filter.

The final step is to reconstruct the galaxy onto the source plane by applying the lens model described in Appendix A. The gravitational magnification of a factor of $\mu\sim 5$ in the central parts of the galaxy delivers a resolution for the IFU data of $\sigma_{psf}=29$ mas $=235$ pc, calculated by casting a PSF placed at the galaxy’s centroid to the source plane (see Appendix B).

## 3 Spatially resolved gas emission

### 3.1 Emission lines fit

In order to isolate emission lines due to ionized gas, we first have to model the underlying emission from the stellar continuum. We fit the stellar continuum contribution in each spaxel using the pPXF code. The model used for the stellar population synthesis with pPXF and the E-MILES library (Vazdekis et al., 2016) is analogous to the one used by Newman et al. (2026). The best-fit stellar continuum model is subtracted from the data to isolate the emission lines. An example spectrum and stellar continuum fit is given in Figure 1. To measure the stellar kinematics, we perform an additional ppxf run in which the strongest emission lines are masked, since tests showed that fitting them could bias the stellar velocity dispersions (Newman et al, in prep.).

All rest-frame optical emission lines – consisting of ${\rm H\alpha}$ , ${\rm H\beta}$ , [OII] $\lambda\lambda 3727,3729$ , [OIII] $\lambda\lambda 5007,4959$ , [NII] $\lambda\lambda 6548,6581$ , [SII] $\lambda\lambda 6717,6732$ , [NeIII] $\lambda 3968$ and [OI] $\lambda 6300$ – are fitted together for each spatial bin. The fitting is performed using EMCEE, an affine invariant Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) ensemble sampler (Foreman-Mackey et al., 2013). We employ single Gaussian profiles fitting the same velocity shift and dispersion for all lines, and taking into account the NIRSpec wavelength-dependent spectral broadening. The flux ratios [OIII]5007/[OIII]4959 and [NII]6581/[NII]6548 are fixed at the theoretical value of 3:1 (Osterbrock and Ferland, 2006). Although our spectral resolution is not sufficiently high to resolve the [OII] $\lambda\lambda 3727,3729$ doublet, we fit the lines separately and impose the $1.5<\mathrm{[OII]3729/[OII]3727}<2.5$ theoretical limits on their flux ratio (Osterbrock and Ferland, 2006).

We then repeat the fit using double Gaussian components for each line profile, in which the kinematics of both components are tied together across all lines during the fit. We do not assign any physical meaning to each Gaussian component, but rather use them to better reproduce the observed line profiles. Finally, for each spatial bin, we select which model better reproduces the data based on residuals and the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) score of the fits. The line surface brightness values provided throughout this paper correspond to the median values from the EMCEE parameters’ posterior distributions, with uncertainties represented by the $\pm 1\sigma$ percentiles around the median values. We consider a line above the detection threshold when it is detected with a signal-to-noise ratio $>3$ .

We find that ionized gas emission is detected across the entire galaxy, with many bins requiring double Gaussian profile to reproduce the observed data. The high spatial resolution highlights interesting features in the ionized gas lines, that make it possible to thoroughly map the kinematics and physical properties of the ionized gas. In Fig. 2, we show the integrated surface brightness maps for the ${\rm H\alpha}$ and [OIII] $\lambda 5007$ emission lines, and we compare the kinematics of the gas emission and the stellar component. ${\rm H\alpha}$ is well detected in all bins, while [OIII] is mostly detected in the central regions and along the minor axis (upper left and upper right panels, respectively). Both lines’ surface brightness distribution peak towards the center, with the brightest bin overlapping the centroid of the galaxy.

### 3.2 Gas kinematics

*Figure 2: Source plane maps of MRG-M0150. First row: integrated surface brightness of the fitted ${\rm H\alpha}$ (left) and [OIII] $\lambda 5007$ emission lines (right); light gray areas mark non-detections. Second row: velocity field of the gas (left) from fitted ${\rm H\alpha}$ line profile, and of the stars (right) from pPXF. Third row: gas (left) and stellar (right) velocity dispersions, obtained in the same way. Maps are rotated to align the x and y axis to the major and minor axis, respectively.*

In the second and third rows of panels in Fig. 2 we compare the velocity and dispersion of the gas (which are taken as the moment 1 and moment 2 of the best-fit profile of the ${\rm H\alpha}$ emission line) to the stellar kinematics. It is immediately visible that the kinematics of stars and ionized gas are not well coupled in this system. The stellar velocity field traces a well defined rotating disk, as already observed by Newman et al. (2018b) (right panel), whereas the gas does not follow at all the stellar rotational pattern, with the red- and blue-shifted sides of the gas velocity field positioned almost perpendicular to the stellar rotational axis. The velocity dispersion field (last row of panels) is also quite different between stars and gas. The gas map shows a symmetric, high-velocity dispersion feature almost aligned with the minor axis of the galaxy that is absent from the stellar map, as well as exhibiting generally higher values of $\sigma$ in the central regions.

The decoupling between stellar and gas velocity field suggests that the gas emission we are detecting is not produced by star-forming regions rotating in the disk, but may instead be coming from a galaxy-wide ionized gas outflow, as commonly observed in AGN host galaxies with the same gas kinematics signature (Fabian, 2012; Fiore et al., 2017). The outflowing gas scenario could also explain the widespread emission from ionized gas observed in this quenched galaxy, in the absence of the star-formation needed to sustain the observed emission. In this case, an outflow centrally driven by an active nucleus would explain both the observed line fluxes and gas kinematics.

### 3.3 Resolved line ratios

We investigate the possibility that MRG-M0150 hosts an AGN by using resolved rest-frame optical line diagnostics, which are widely used to discern between the contributions of star formation (SF) and AGN emission to the ionization of the interstellar medium (ISM). In the top panel of Fig. 3 we show the BPT diagram (Baldwin et al., 1981), i.e., [OIII]/H $\beta$ as a function of [NII]/ ${\rm H\alpha}$ , for each spatial bin in which all lines are detected. The resolved BPT diagram of MRG-M0150 indicates the presence of ionizing radiation that is not due to star formation: as noticeable in the upper panel of Fig. 3, all spatial bins for which all 4 emission lines are detected – colored in the map on the right – are clustered in the same region of the BPT diagram. Line ratios typical of Low Ionization Nuclear Emission-line Regions (LINERs) are detected from the center to the edges of the galaxy. LINER-like ratios can arise from AGN photoionization (Ho, 2008, e.g.), shocked gas (Dopita et al., 2015, e.g.) or ionization by hot evolved stellar populations (Belfiore et al., 2016, e.g.) and the BPT diagram alone cannot definitively differentiate between excitation mechanisms.

We construct the resolved WHaN diagram (Cid Fernandes et al., 2011) by showing the equivalent width (EW) of ${\rm H\alpha}$ as a function of [NII]/ ${\rm H\alpha}$ ,in Fig. 3, lower left panel. The WHaN diagram is useful to identify regions of gas ionized by hot evolved stellar populations, such as post-AGB stars, which can heavily contribute to the total ionizing flux budget particularly in quiescent galaxies (Cid Fernandes et al., 2010). We find that most of the spatial bins in MRG-M0150 are located above the “retired galaxy” line at 3 Å in ${\rm H\alpha}$ EW (Cid Fernandes et al., 2011): this implies that most of the observed emission is not excited by ionization due to old stars, but instead a contribution from AGN radiation or shocks is needed to explain the observations. Furthermore, Byler et al. (2019) found that the EW of H $\alpha$ line emission due to post-AGB stars is weaker for younger stellar populations (stellar ages $<1$ Gyr), shifting down the retired galaxies threshold for high-z quiescent galaxies. Estimating the contribution of shocks from AGN or star-formation feedback to the total ionizing budget of MRG-M0150 is a more difficult endeavor. The negligible level of current star formation in this galaxy, as inferred from ${\rm H\alpha}$ luminosity (Sect. 3.4), makes it unlikely that shocks from star formation feedback are the main source of ionization. Instead, the observed LINER-like line ratios are more likely to be due to AGN photoionization or shocks from a central AGN-driven outflow.

We map the ${\rm H\alpha}$ EW distribution across the galaxy in the lower-right panel of Fig. 3: unlike the ${\rm H\alpha}$ surface brightness map in Fig. 2, the ${\rm H\alpha}$ EW is higher in the outskirts of the galaxy than in the center. This radial trend cannot be explained by gradients in star formation or dust attenuation, given that the line ratios show little indication of either (Sect. 3.4). It is also inconsistent with hot, evolved stars powering the line emission, since in that case the line emission should more closely follow the stellar light. Instead, we propose that the ${\rm H\alpha}$ EW pattern is analogous to that seen in ’red geysers’, a category that represents $\sim 10\%$ of all massive quiescent galaxies at $z\sim 0$ . Red geyser galaxies are characterized by the presence of a low-luminosity AGN (LL-AGN) in their center and centrally-driven ionized gas outflows (Cheung et al., 2016; Roy et al., 2021). In these galaxies, the same ${\rm H\alpha}$ EW pattern is due to the fact that the ${\rm H\alpha}$ emission is tracing the outflowing gas, while the continuum is tracing the stellar population: going from the center to the outskirts of the galaxy, the stellar surface brightness profile decreases more rapidly then the ${\rm H\alpha}$ emissivity in the outflow, generating the observed inside-out EW distribution. The distribution of ${\rm H\alpha}$ EW in MRG-M0150 is thus further evidence in support of the presence of a centrally-driven, galaxy-wide ionized gas outflow.

### 3.4 Residual star formation and AGN activity in MRG-M0150

Although line ratio diagnostics and gas kinematics indicate that the line emission is not powered by star formation, we can still use the integrated ${\rm H\alpha}$ line luminosity to place an upper limit on the residual star formation rate. We obtain the total integrated ${\rm H\alpha}$ flux by first correcting the flux measured in each spaxel for magnification, and then correcting for dust attenuation. In a small number of bins (13 out of 61) where both ${\rm H\alpha}$ and ${\rm H\beta}$ lines are above the detection limit of $3\sigma$ , we are able to use the Balmer decrement ${\rm H\alpha}$ / ${\rm H\beta}$ to estimate the dust attenuation AV; for all other bins, we use the value estimated by the pPXF fits. We find generally low dust attenuation throughout the galaxy using both methods, with a median value of A ${}_{V}=0.3_{-0.3}^{+0.4}$ . We then apply the Calzetti et al. (2000) dust attenuation curve and obtain the unabsorbed ${\rm H\alpha}$ luminosity. Assuming the conversion provided by Kennicutt (1998), we derive a current SFR for MRG-M0150 of $0.30\pm 0.08$ M⊙ yr-1, which has to be considered an upper limit on the true SFR of the galaxy, since most of the ${\rm H\alpha}$ emission is excited by processes other than star formation, according to the diagnostics of Fig. 3. For a galaxy of stellar mass $\log(M/M_{\odot})=11.30$ , this implies a specific star-formation rate of $\log(\text{sSFR/yr}^{-1})=-11.8$ . This is very strong evidence of the currently quenched nature of the galaxy, and confirms the presence of an AGN in the center of the galaxy as the main engine powering the observed ionized gas emission.

We investigate the AGN properties by estimating its bolometric luminosity using the [O III] 5007 line luminosity in the central spaxel, corrected for aperture losses assuming a point-like emission. We correct for dust attenuation using the Balmer decrement and compute a central [O III] luminosity of $L_{\rm[O\penalty\ III]}=(9\pm 2)\cdot 10^{39}$ erg s-1. Assuming the bolometric correction factor from Heckman et al. (2004), we derive the AGN bolometric luminosity $L_{\rm bol}=(3.2\pm 0.9)\cdot 10^{43}$ erg s-1. We estimate the Eddington luminosity of the SMBH from the black hole mass, which we infer from the M ${}_{\rm BH}-\sigma$ relation of McConnell et al. (2011), adopting the light-weighted second stellar velocity moment within the effective radius to define $\sigma=282$ km s-1. We find an Eddington ratio of $L_{\rm bol}/L_{\rm Edd}\approx 10^{-3.8}$ . Using the [O III] line luminosity integrated over the whole galaxy – as might be done for unresolved studies – yields a bolometric AGN luminosity almost $6\times$ higher.

We further constrained $L_{\rm bol}$ using a 27 ks observation with the Advanced CCD Imaging Spectrometer (ACIS) onboard the Chandra X-ray Observatory (program 11800090, PI H. Ebeling). We used the same methodology as Newman et al. (2026) to measure $L_{X}$ , which we define from $2-10$ keV in the rest frame, and to estimate $L_{\rm bol}=C_{X}L_{X}$ using $C_{X}=15.8$ (Ho, 2009). For the multiple images 1, 2, and 3, we find $L_{\rm bol}/10^{44}\penalty\ {\rm erg}\penalty\ {\rm s}^{-1}=1.3\pm 1.2$ , $2.9\pm 2.3$ , and $5.1\pm 1.9$ , respectively. We thus marginally detect X-ray emission in each image. We combined the Poisson posteriors for $L_{\rm bol}$ from the three multiple images to estimate $L_{\rm bol}=3.3^{+1.2}_{-1.0}\cdot 10^{44}\penalty\ {\rm erg}\penalty\ {\rm s}^{-1}$ . This is an order of magnitude higher than [O III]-based estimate, which could be an underestimate due to the LINER-type spectrum. Nonetheless, the implied Eddington ratio is still low, $L_{\rm bol}/L_{\rm Edd}\approx 10^{-2.8}$ .

The low bolometric luminosity and Eddington ratio classifies the SMBH as an LL-AGN, a class of AGN occupying the faintest end of the luminosity function and characterized by very low accretion rates, $L_{\rm bol}/L_{\rm Edd}\leq 10^{-3}$ (see Ho, 2008, for a review). Recent studies of similar quenched systems at cosmic noon and even higher redshift have found a high incidence of LL-AGN activity (Bugiani et al., 2025; Skarbinski et al., 2026) based on rest-frame optical line diagnostics.

### 4.1 Wind model

All the evidence so far points to the presence of an AGN-driven galaxy-wide ionized gas outflow originating from the central part of the galaxy. To test whether our observations are compatible with such model we employ the kinematics fitting code “Modeling Outflows and Kinematics of AGN in 3D” (Marconcini et al., 2023, MOKA3D;) and apply it to the de-lensed maps of observed emission line profiles. MOKA3D reconstructs the three-dimensional gas distribution in the outflow by weighting model emitting clouds according to the observed line emission profile and velocity in each spaxel (Sect.3.1). It then generates a model data cube with the same spatial and spectral resolution as the observations, including PSF convolution. This tomographic reconstruction enables the geometry and kinematics of the outflow to be constrained, and provides estimates of its mass outflow rate and energetics.

The model adopted is shown in Fig. 4a. We assume a bi-conical geometry for the wind, with a semi-aperture angle of 45 degrees consistent with other AGN-driven outflows studied at lower or equal redshift. The origin is fixed in the brightest spaxel in the [OIII] emission line map, co-spatial with the geometric center of the galaxy, and the position angle of the bi-cone’s axis is fixed to $-$ 5 degrees with respect to the minor axis after visual inspection of the observed gas velocity distribution. We adopt a constant radial velocity profile in both the receding and the approaching cones, which are fitted independently from each other. For each cone, we find best-fit values of radial velocity $v_{out}$ and inclination angle $\beta$ , defined as the angle between the cone’s axis and the observer’s direction, of the wind in 5 shells of incremental radius, as shown in Fig. 4a. Global values for the inclination and intrinsic velocity of the wind in the cone are given by averaging the values obtained in the shells. We repeat the fit twice – once fitting the emission line profiles of the [OIII] line and once with ${\rm H\alpha}$ – and find consistent results. Further details on the 3D kinematics modeling of the gas emission in MRG-M0150 are provided in Appendix B.

### 4.2 Outflow properties and energetics

The results of the MOKA3D modeling using the ${\rm H\alpha}$ line profiles and a bi-conical wind prescription are summarized in Fig. 4. Analogous results and plots for the [OIII] line fitting results can be found in Appendix B. The gas kinematics are well reproduced by the model, as visible from the residuals map. The observations match a bi-conical wind whose axis is nearly within the plane of the sky: a schematic representation of the geometry of the outflow with respect to the stellar disk and our line-of-sight is shown in Fig. 5. For the approaching $(+)$ side, we find an inclination angle $\beta=80$ degrees with respect to the line-of-sight and an intrinsic de-projected velocity of $v_{+}=1200\pm 57$ km s-1; for the receding $(-)$ side an inclination angle $\beta=100$ degrees and similar velocity $v_{+}=1150\pm 49$ km s-1. Consistent results are obtained from the model fitted to the [OIII] line emission, although we measure slightly lower values of wind velocity (see Table 1). The two cones extend out to the edge of the fitted spaxels, corresponding to an extension of at least 3.3 kpc ( $2.3$ times the effective radius $R_{e}$ in F444W).

As visible in Fig. 5, the bi-conical outflow’s inclination implies strong interactions between the galaxy’s disk and the outflow. This is not often seen in classical QSOs and starburst systems hosting such large-scale ionized phase winds (Veilleux et al., 2005), as usually the outflow chooses the path of least resistance out of the galaxy and is seen positioned perpendicular to the disk plane. The quiescent nature of MRG-M0150 may be a contributor to the relative orientation of the outflow and the disk: indeed, a centrally-driven wind expanding inside a quiescent system with a negligible amount of gas in its disk does not encounter much resistance from the ISM along its path and is free to propagate in any direction. This is the case for MRG-M0150, for which ALMA observations of the dust continuum (Whitaker et al., 2021, REQUIEM survey,) give an upper limit of 1% on its molecular gas fraction. Interestingly, recent semi-analytical models of dust evolution in quiescent galaxies find that AGN feedback can rapidly destroy dust in after quenching (Donevski et al., 2026), in line with both the ALMA results and the AGN activity detected in MRG-M0150. On the other hand, the close alignment between the outflow axis and the stellar disk could favor strong interactions between the wind and the ISM, contributing to a negative feedback mechanism. The higher residuals between model and observations in the moment 2 (fig. 4, bottom right panel) reflects closely the feature of enhanced gas velocity dispersion of Fig. 2 and may be tracing injected turbulence by the wind in the densest ISM regions as a consequence of wind-disk interactions.

*Figure 8: Radial velocity profile of the ionized gas outflows in MRG-M0150, according to the 3D kinematics fit. The left panel shows the profile for the approaching (blue) and receding (red) sides of the bi-conical outflow derived from [OIII]; the right one shows the values derived from ${\rm H\alpha}$ .*

We use the model to constrain the wind’s mass outflow rate and energetics, following Marconcini et al. (2023). The tomographical reconstruction of emission clouds in the outflow by the MOKA3D code enables us to accurately estimate the mass outflow rate of the ionized phase outflow and to better constrain wind energetics with respect to standard approaches used when the outflow physical properties are unknown (Carniani et al., 2015; Cano-Díaz et al., 2012). But first, we need to estimate an electron density $n_{e}$ . This is usually derived using either the [OII] $\lambda\lambda 3727,3729$ or the [SII] $\lambda\lambda 6717,6732$ doublet ratio (Osterbrock and Ferland, 2006), or is assumed from a broad range of values – from $1000$ cm-3 (Venturi et al., 2025; Bertola et al., 2025) to more widely adopted choices of $n_{e}\sim 100-200$ cm-3 (Kakkad et al., 2016; Brusa et al., 2015; Cresci et al., 2015b; Fiore et al., 2017, e.g.). We infer the average electron density of the gas in the red- and blue-shifted sides of the outflow from the observed [SII] $\lambda\lambda 6717,6732$ doublet ratio, since the [OII] doublet is not resolved at NIRSpec’s medium spectral resolution. The most rigorous approach involves deriving a resolved map of the [SII] doublet ratio to infer $n_{e}$ in each spaxel: however, the [SII] doublet is below detection limit for many bins of the cube, on top of being difficult to de-blend in most of the rest. Thus, we choose to adopt a constant electron density value $n_{e}=600$ cm-3 for both sides of the wind, corresponding to the average value found in all spaxels with an accurate estimate of the [SII] doublet ratio, assuming a temperature of $10^{4}$ K. This choice constitutes one of the most important sources of uncertainties in the outflow’s energetics estimation – indeed, assuming a constant electron density can significantly impact the outflow energetics (Davies et al., 2020a; Veilleux et al., 2020) – thus, we attach a 50% systematic uncertainty to $n_{e}$ to account both for the averaging procedure and the uniform density assumptions. Moreover, different values adopted for the constant electron density only affect the (inverse) scaling of the mass outflow rate $\dot{M}_{out}$ and related quantities by a numerical factor; thus our inferred $n_{e}=600$ cm-3 results in more conservative $\dot{M}_{out}$ values than the typical assumptions of $n_{e}\sim 100-200$ cm-3 would yield.

We finally obtain a total mass outflow rate from the ionized gas of $0.08\pm 0.02$ M⊙ yr-1 from the [OIII] line flux, and $0.6\pm 0.2$ M⊙ yr-1 from the ${\rm H\alpha}$ line flux. This discrepancy in mass outflow rate values between [OIII] and Balmer lines tracers is a consequence of the different volumes in which [OIII] and ${\rm H\alpha}$ are emitted: [OIII] is a higher-ionization tracer that usually misses a substantial amount of lower-ionized gas mass (Carniani et al., 2015), especially in LINERs such as MRG-M0150. Furthermore, no dust correction was applied to the line luminosities before calculations, thus [OIII] may be more affected by attenuation than the redder ${\rm H\alpha}$ line, as well as being under the detection limit in many spaxels embedded in the outflow (see Fig.14 in Appendix B). Thus, we adopt the mass outflow rates and derived properties given by ${\rm H\alpha}$ as our fiducial values. Consequently, we can calculate the energy and momentum rates of the ionized wind as:

$$ \displaystyle\dot{E}_{kin}=\frac{1}{2}\dot{M}_{out}v_{out}^{2}=(2.8\pm 0.2)\cdot 10^{41}\text{ erg s}^{-1} \displaystyle\dot{p}_{out}=\dot{M}_{out}v_{out}=(5\pm 2)\cdot 10^{33}\text{ dyne} $$

All the derived outflow energetics are summed up in Table 1.

### 4.3 Alternative models

We also consider a tilted gaseous disk geometry to explain the observed emission. To test this scenario, we use MOKA3D to fit a rotating disk model to the observed ${\rm H\alpha}$ line emission, allowing it to be freely inclined with respect to the stellar disk. We find that the rotating disk model requires extreme rotational velocities of $v_{rot}\sim 600$ km s-1 and an inclination of the gas disk of 80 degrees. Thus, we can exclude this model from the discussion. We also experiment with an alternative model in which we constrain the inclination angle of the bi-cone to be $30^{\circ}$ , in order to simulate a (more commonly observed) nearly-polar bi-cone with a 3D outflow velocity more comparable to the observed projected one. We find, however, that such model does a poor job in fitting the observed data (see Appendix B).

## 5 SED fitting and star-formation history

We carry out full SED fitting on the integrated photometry and spectroscopy of MRG-M0150 using Prospector (Johnson et al., 2021), to reconstruct its star-formation history (SFH) and verify the quenched state of the galaxy. The integrated photometry and spectrum are extracted from all spatial bins included in the analysis, corresponding to an aperture of $2.3\text{ R}_{e}$ . Flux values extracted in each spaxel are corrected for magnification according to the lens model before being added together, and an additional $10\%$ error is added in quadrature to all photometric points to account for systematic uncertainties.

We employ a model akin to the one used in Park et al. (2024), adopting MIST isochrones (Dotter, 2016), the MILES stellar library (Falcón-Barroso et al., 2011), and a non-parametric star-formation history (SFH) defined on 14 logarithmically-spaced age bins. A “continuity prior” on the SFH is adopted, which discourages drastic variations of SFR between adjacent time bins (Leja et al., 2019). We fit photometry from the ACS/WFC F814W filter and JWST/NIRCam’s F115W, F200W, F277W, F444W filters, together with the integrated spectrum from NIRSpec/IFU in the $4000-6700$ Å wavelength range. Given that nebular emission lines are tracing the AGN activity and/or the outflowing gas and not star formation, we choose to marginalize over them during the fit. We do not include any AGN emission in the model.

The quality of the photometry + spectrum fitting is shown in Fig. 6. In Fig. 7, we plot MRG-M0150’s non-parametric star formation history derived by Prospector (green line). This is compared to our upper limit on the current SFR measured from the integrated ${\rm H\alpha}$ luminosity (red diamond) and to the mass outflow rate of the ionized gas outflow (blue squares). The reconstructed SFH of MRG-M0150 is similar to other recently quenched systems observed at $z>2$ (Park et al., 2024; Carnall et al., 2023b; Belli et al., 2024), showing a sharp decrease of the SFR after the peak at $\sim 500$ Myr ago in lookback time. We further discuss the SFH of MRG-M0150 and the impact of outflows in Sect. 6.4.
