We have detected widespread line emission throughout MRG-M0150. Given the upper limit on the residual star formation from H $\alpha$ and the observed emission line ratios, we concluded that the ionized gas emission is not powered by star formation but instead requires an AGN contribution. Moreover, the bi-conical, centrally-driven outflow morphology and its inclination with respect to the stellar disk (Fig. 5) further argues against a stellar origin of the observed winds, which would produce a much different wind geometry (see Veilleux et al., 2005, for examples). Finally, the velocities we measure are substantially higher than what observed in the most powerful star-formation driven outflows at $z\sim 2$ (Davies et al., 2019). Thus, we conclude an AGN in MRG-M0150 is driving the observed outflow, for which we measure a mass outflow rate of $0.6\pm 0.2$ $\rm M_{\odot}\penalty\ yr^{-1}$ .

### 6.1 Recently launched ionized gas outflows from a LL-AGN

Thanks to the high spatial resolution achieved by NIRSpec, the lensing magnification in MRG-M0150, and our ionized wind kinematics fitting, we can use this system to directly measure the timescales of an AGN-driven outflow in a quiescent galaxy at $z>2$ . In Fig. 8, we plot the radial wind velocity along both the blue-shifted and red-shifted sides of the bi-conical outflow as fitted by MOKA3D using the [OIII] emission line and the H $\alpha$ line. We find ionized gas velocities $v_{\rm out}\sim 1200$ km s-1, similar to those of prototypical Seyfert galaxies (Fiore et al., 2017) and much higher than the $v_{\rm out}\sim 300-400$ km s-1 usually observed in the local “red geyser” galaxies, but consistent with ionized-phase outflow velocities found in similar massive, quenched galaxies at cosmic noon, such as Belli et al. (2024) and D’Eugenio et al. (2024). These results suggest a difference in the nature of feedback mechanisms and impact of ionized gas outflows in massive quiescent systems between $z>2$ and $z=0$ .

Using the radial velocity profile of the wind in MRG-M0150, we can constrain the launching timescales of the observed wind. Considering the full extent of the wind, we infer that the ionized outflow in MRG-M0150 has been launched over, at least, the past $2.6$ Myr. Narrowing our focus on the innermost shell of the bicone and using the lowest measured velocity from the [OIII] line fit, we infer that the innermost resolved portion of the wind must have launched no more than $\sim 0.45$ Myr ago from the nuclear region: this shows that the central engine has been recently launching material. Moreover, the SFH inferred by the SED fitting (Fig.7) further rules out a fossil origin for the observed outflow due to a past starburst, given that the travel times that we measure for the bi-conical winds are much smaller than the time elapsed since the last burst in star formation ( $\sim 500$ Myr). The biconical and centrally-driven outflow geometry in MRG-M0150 also differs from that predicted for fossil AGN outflows, which hydrodynamical simulations show to become detached from the nucleus, lopsided and slow once the driving AGN has switched off (Zubovas and Maskeliūnas, 2023).

Following Davies et al. (2024) and Taylor et al. (2026), in Figure 9 we compare the wind energetics to the AGN bolometric luminosity for MRG-M0150. We also show the ionized outflows reported in the literature for Cosmic-Noon AGN – as compiled by Venturi et al. (2025), converted to $n_{e}\sim 600$ cm-3 (green triangles) – as well as those observed in two massive quiescent galaxies at $z>2$ by Belli et al. (2024) and D’Eugenio et al. (2024), and in the prototype red geyser “Akira” (Cheung et al., 2016). Energy-conserving AGN-driven outflows carry kinetic energy rates to up to $5\%$ of the AGN bolometric luminosity (King and Pounds, 2015), while their momentum rate $\dot{p}_{out}=L_{BOL}/c$ can be boosted by a factor of 5-20 due to interactions with the ISM (Faucher-Giguère and Quataert, 2012): we mark these theoretical limits with black dashed lines in the plots. As expected, we find substantially different energy and momentum rates when using ${\rm H\alpha}$ rather then [OIII] (see Sect.4.2), however in both cases we find that the system is broadly consistent with an extrapolation of the Venturi et al. (2025) outflows to lower $L_{\rm bol}$ , and within the theoretical limits expected given the power of the central engine. MRG-M0150’s outflow energy and momentum rates (from ${\rm H\alpha}$ ) are consistent with those found in the other two quiescent galaxies at high-z, even though they host AGN $\sim 2$ dex more luminous. Since outflow properties for both of these objects have been estimated using [OIII] emission, a substantial fraction of mass outflow in the ionized phase may be missed by relying only on higher-ionization lines. Thus, especially in the case of LL-AGN hosted in quiescent galaxies, mass outflow rates and related properties estimated from [OIII] should be treated as lower limits on the true values. We also note that the X-ray-based estimate of $L_{\rm bol}$ is about an order of magnitude higher than the [OIII]-based one (Sect. 3.4), so that the ratio between the outflow energetics and the AGN luminosity decreases by about one dex when the former is adopted. We conclude that the current LL-AGN in MRG-M0150 is powerful enough to sustain the observed winds, and that a previous, more luminous AGN episode is not required by the energetics.

### 6.2 Incidence of ionized gas outflows

The incidence of AGN-driven ionized gas outflows in high-z massive quiescent galaxies appears to be relatively high. In particular, Bugiani et al. (2025) report an incidence of $\sim 20\%$ , and comparable values are found by studies targeting outflows in the neutral phase (Sapori et al., 2026; Davies et al., 2024). This is higher than what is found in the local Universe – in which the red geyser galaxies constitute around $10\%$ of the entire quiescent population – indicating that ionized gas outflows in high-z quiescent galaxies are not only more powerful but also more frequent than in their local counterparts. Interestingly, our detection of the ionized outflows in MRG-M0150 is highly dependent on the availability of both lensed and spatially resolved data. To illustrate this, we simulate the unlensed and unresolved NIRSpec/MSA spectrum of the target with a slit loss of $\sim 50\%$ by extracting the integrated spectrum within 1 $R_{e}$ of the galaxy, corrected for magnification: when fitting the emission lines in this spectrum, the broad component is no longer statistically preferred over a single-component model (see the BIC values for both fits in Fig. 10), implying that such outflows may remain undetected in unresolved observations of high-z galaxies. The same applies to the X-ray emission of the central LL-AGN, which is only marginally detected in each of the multiple images (Sect. 3.4). This suggests that the relatively high incidence of outflows previously reported is a lower limit, supporting the idea that winds driven by a LL-AGN are a common phase in the evolution of massive quiescent galaxies at cosmic noon, while they become rarer in the present-day Universe.

### 6.3 The fossil outflow scenario

The relationship between the observed multiphase outflows in massive galaxies at $z>2$ and the low levels of AGN activity observed in the same sample remains unclear, as these AGN are rarely detected in X-rays and are primarily classified as active through rest-frame optical diagnostic diagrams (Bugiani et al., 2025; Skarbinski et al., 2026). Studies of neutral-phase outflows in massive galaxies at high redshift have raised the idea that these constitute mostly relics of a past starburst or fossils of past quasar events – that is, short-lived bursts of black-hole activity that occurred at earlier epochs than the time of observation (Taylor et al., 2026; Almaini et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2026). The remnant nature of outflows observed in high-z quenched galaxies hosting inactive or low-luminosity AGN is supported by hydrodynamical simulations (Zubovas et al., 2022, e.g.) and energetics arguments (Almaini et al., 2025; Taylor et al., 2026), which for many of the observed galaxies struggle to reconcile the lack of powerful AGN signatures with the energetics of the observed neutral-phase winds (while ionized-phase winds generally do not pose a problem, as shown in Fig. 9). In this scenario, the low incidence of X-ray AGN among recently quenched galaxies at cosmic noon ( $\sim 6\%$ ; Almaini et al. 2025) is reconciled with the high incidence of fast outflows if the luminous AGN phase is short-lived, while the outflow it launches remains visible for up to $\sim 10$ Myr after the AGN has faded (Almaini et al., 2025). For example, Taylor et al. (2026) assume that the detection rate of neutral outflows/inflows in quenched galaxies from the EXCELS survey is set by the duty cycle timescales of the AGN hosted at their center, and conclude that the visibility window of both an X-ray active AGN and the outflow launched by the same event is extremely short, of the order of 1 Myr.

It is useful to distinguish between two versions of the fossil outflow scenario. In its weaker form, it postulates that the outflows observed today were often launched by an AGN in a substantially different state from the one we observe, so that the present-day $L_{\rm bol}$ is poorly correlated with the wind energetics, even if a lower-luminosity AGN is still active. A single galaxy whose outflow does not exceed the energy budget of its current AGN, such as MRG-M0150, cannot test this version. In its stronger form, the AGN switches between “on” and “off” states, or at least undergoes drastic changes in $L_{\rm bol}$ , and only the “on” phases are able to drive outflows. MRG-M0150 can be used as a test case for this second version.

Our kinematic modelling shows that the innermost portion of the wind was launched no more than $\sim 0.45$ Myr ago, well within the 1 Myr time window in which an outflow and the X-ray bright AGN that launched it should be observable at the same time (Taylor et al., 2026). We do detect the AGN, but it is a LL-AGN with $\lambda_{Edd}\approx 10^{-3}$ (Sect. 3.4) almost an order of magnitude below the Eddington ratio adopted by Taylor et al. (2026) as the threshold for X-ray detection and for AGN activity capable of driving outflows ( $\lambda\gtrsim 0.027$ ). This suggests that AGN in a lower accretion state can also launch and sustain galaxy-scale winds. Such systems are, however, difficult to identify: neither the AGN nor the ionized outflow in MRG-M0150 would have been detected without lensing and spatially resolved spectroscopy (Sect. 6.2), and in unlensed, unresolved samples, galaxies like MRG-M0150 would likely be counted as hosting neither. Accounting for this population may therefore lengthen the inferred overlap between the AGN duty cycle and outflow phases.

The energetics argument in favor of fossil outflows is also sensitive to how $L_{\rm bol}$ is estimated. In most quiescent galaxies at these redshifts, $L_{\rm bol}$ can only be derived from the [OIII] line, an estimate subject to significant systematic uncertainties related to dust obscuration and to the physical state of the AGN (Taylor et al., 2026, see the discussion in). In MRG-M0150, the X-ray-based $L_{\rm bol}$ is an order of magnitude higher than our [OIII]-based estimate (Sect. 3.4). If similar offsets apply to other LL-AGN in quiescent galaxies, their current AGN may account for a larger fraction of the observed outflow energetics than [OIII]-based estimates would suggest.

These considerations suggest an interpretation in which the AGN luminosity in quenched galaxies follows a continuous distribution that declines after quenching, rather than alternating between two distinct states. The AGN may flicker on short timescales, but its overall luminosity fades as the galaxy ages, as also illustrated by the scenario proposed by Almaini et al. (2025), in which AGN activity broadly traces the decline of the SFR after the starburst. Consistently, Valentino et al. (2026) find that the most luminous AGN in quenched galaxies at $z\sim 1.5-4.5$ are preferentially found in the youngest post-starburst systems. Observed shortly after quenching, galaxies such as COSMOS-11142 (Belli et al., 2024) host massive outflows and luminous AGN. MRG-M0150 would represent a later stage, in which both the AGN and the outflow have faded below the sensitivity of typical unlensed observations. Finally, older quiescent galaxies show no outflows and, in some cases, evidence of gas accretion, as in the lensed galaxy MRG-M0138 (Gangula et al., 2026). Within this framework, MRG-M0150 shows that AGN just below the detection limits of current samples can still drive galaxy-scale outflows. Such weak activity may be common: stacking the X-ray emission of individually undetected post-starburst galaxies at cosmic noon reveals, on average, low-level AGN accretion ( $L/L_{\rm Edd}\lesssim 10^{-3}$ ; Almaini et al. 2025).

### 6.4 Quenching by AGN-driven outflows

A major open question regarding observations of gas outflows in high-redshift quiescent galaxies is whether the presence of these winds can be directly linked to the quenching of the galaxy itself. While it is not trivial to link the rapid quenching of MRG-M0150 in the last 0.5 Gyr with the observed ionized-phase outflows, the mass outflow rate of $0.6\pm 0.2$ M⊙ yr-1 is higher than the current levels of SF, for which we have an upper limit of 0.30 M⊙ yr-1 from H $\alpha$ , consistent with the SFR estimated by Prospector in the most recent time bin of [0–30] Myr (SFR $=0.2^{+0.2}_{-0.8}$ M⊙ yr-1, see Fig. 7). Furthermore, the detection of outflowing neutral gas through the Na D absorption line in the central parts of the galaxy (Gangula et al., in prep.) implies a multi-phase nature of the observed winds. It has been observed that neutral-phase gas can reach mass outflow rates more than one order of magnitude higher than in the ionized phase, both at high redshift (Belli et al., 2024) and in the local Universe (Roberts-Borsani, 2020; Avery et al., 2022). Thus, the ionized-phase mass outflow rate that we measure is a strictly lower limit on the true rate of the multiphase wind in MRG-M0150.

The high velocities reached by the ionized outflow means that some of the gas may be capable of escaping the gravitational potential of the galaxy. The halo escape velocity is expected to be 2.5–3 times the rotational velocity of the galaxy (Weiner et al., 2009; Swinbank et al., 2019, e.g.). Using the rotational velocity of MRG-M0150 inferred from stellar kinematic modelling of $v_{\rm rot}\approx 450$ km s-1 (Newman et al., in prep.), we estimate an escape velocity between $\sim 1100-1300\rm\penalty\ km\penalty\ s^{-1}$ . The highest velocities measured in the ionized outflow are comparable to these estimates, suggesting that a substantial amount of ionized outflowing gas may be able to escape the halo. This type of “ejective” feedback from AGN-driven outflows has been invoked also in the post-starburst high- $z$ galaxies of Belli et al. (2024) and D’Eugenio et al. (2024), in which the ejection of cold gas at a faster rate than it can be converted into stars has been invoked as the main mechanism through which the galaxy has been quenched. While the fast-moving ionized phase does not transport as much mass as the cold phase, what we observe in MRG-M0150 and similar high- $z$ systems is qualitatively different than the “maintenance mode” feedback of local red geysers, in which the ionized-phase gas is unable to escape the galaxy and instead keeps the galaxy quenched through the heating of gas in the halo (Cheung et al., 2016).

Although the short launching timescales associated with the current wind prevents us from directly attributing the main quenching event to the observed outflow, the ongoing wind provides evidence that AGN feedback remains active well after star-formation has been quenched. Outflows such as the one observed here can be intermittent, and it is possible that similar, possibly more powerful episodes have occurred repeatedly since the last peak of star formation. The cumulative effect of recurrent AGN-driven winds, rather than a single event, may therefore have been ultimately responsible for quenching MRG-M0150. The mass outflow rate we measure exceeds the residual SFR, suggesting that winds driven by a low-luminosity AGN can substantially affect the remaining gas reservoir and suppress subsequent star formation well after the initial “blowout” phase. Given that most of an active galaxy’s lifetime is spent in a low-accretion state (Ho, 2008), this type of long-term feedback may represent the key to maintenance of quiescence in massive systems over much longer timescales, potentially linking the population of recently quenched galaxies at cosmic noon to the massive quiescent population observed in the local Universe.

## 7 Summary and conclusions

We have used JWST/NIRSpec IFU observations of the gravitationally lensed massive quiescent galaxy MRG-M0150 at $z=2.64$ , from the INQUEST-JWST sample. Owing to the spatial resolution and sensitivity of NIRSpec’s IFU and the magnification offered by the strong lensing, we are able for the first time to reconstruct in 3D the bi-conical ionized outflow of a massive quiescent galaxy at $z>2$ , making it possible investigate the impact of AGN-driven outflows on star-formation quenching at high redshift. The main findings of this study are the following:

- • MRG-M0150 hosts a previously undetected low-luminosity AGN, identified through LINER-like line ratios and marginal X-ray detections, with $L_{\rm bol}\approx 3\times 10^{43}-3\times 10^{44}$ erg s-1 and $L/L_{\rm Edd}\sim 10^{-3}$ .

- • The ionized gas traces a galaxy-wide, centrally driven bi-conical outflow reaching $\sim 1200$ km s-1, whose mass outflow rate is substantially underestimated when relying only on high-ionization lines such as [OIII] as opposed to low-ionization lines such as ${\rm H\alpha}$ .

- • The outflow has been recently launched by the central LL-AGN: its innermost portion was launched no more than 0.45 Myr ago, and the current AGN is powerful enough to sustain it without requiring a previous, more luminous episode.

- • Neither the AGN nor the outflow would be detected without lensing and spatially resolved spectroscopy, suggesting that similar systems are missed in unresolved samples, affecting incidence-based estimates of the visibility timescales of AGN and outflows.

- • The ionized mass outflow rate ( $0.6\pm 0.2$ M⊙ yr-1), a lower limit on the multiphase wind, exceeds the residual SFR ( $<0.30$ M⊙ yr-1), and part of the gas may escape the halo, implying ejective feedback is still active in the galaxy after the main quenching event. Combined with the relatively high incidence of such outflows, our results suggest that low-luminosity AGN activity may provide an important long-term mechanism for maintaining quiescence in massive galaxies at cosmic noon, potentially over cosmological timescales.

Overall, our work shows that AGN-driven galaxy-wide outflows can be sustained by low-luminosity AGN in massive quiescent galaxies at cosmic noon. These outflows may play a key role in the maintenance of quiescence over long timescales, and are sufficiently common to likely represent a major mechanism in preventing new star-formation in massive galaxies at this epoch. At the same time, our results highlight the importance of spatially resolved spectroscopy, combined with the magnification provided by gravitational lensing, for uncovering and constraining such outflows in the high-redshift Universe.

## Appendix A Lens Model

The modeling was performed using imaging data of the foreground lensing cluster MACSJ0150.3-1005 at $z=0.365$ in the NIRCam F200W bands obtained as part of the same Cycle 3 JWST program that provided the spectroscopic data discussed in the text. Additionally, we identified the cluster members and measured their redshifts making use of the IFU spectroscopic data taken with the Multi Unit Spectroscopic Explorer (MUSE) at the Very Large Telescope (VLT), which covers a field of view of $1\arcmin\times 1\arcmin$ . MACSJ0150.3-1005 was observed in September 2019 for one OB of 48 min (program 0103.A-0777, PI: A. Edge). We reduced the MUSE data and measured the redshifts following the procedure described in Bolamperti et al. (2024).

*Figure 11: Lens model of the MACS J0150 cluster. We show the JWST/NIRCam F115W/F200W/F277W images with an asinh stretch. The three images of MRG-M0150 are labeled; red curves trace the critical line.*

We construct the strong lensing model using the software Gravity.jl (Lombardi, 2024), which allows for the reconstruction of the total mass distribution of the cluster using a multiplane approach. The F200W image of the cluster and multiple images of MRG-M0150, together with the final lens model, can be seen in Figure 11. The following mass components were included into the model. The main cluster-scale DM halo of the cluster, which is parametrized with a nearly isothermal ellipsoid (NIE) mass distribution characterized by six free parameters: the on-sky coordinates (two parameters), ellipticity, position angle, velocity dispersion, and core radius. An elliptical coreless Jaffe profile is used to describe one of the cluster galaxies lying close to Image 2 of MRG-M0150 along the line of sight. Contrary to the NIE profile, its core radius is substituted with a truncation radius, and the galaxy on-sky coordinates are fixed, for a total of 4 free parameters. A second elliptical coreless Jaffe profile with 4 free parameters is used to parameterize a galaxy located in the background at $z=0.4907$ (as determined from the NIRSpec IFU data) that is close in projection to Image 1 of MRG-M0150. This galaxy is included in the model employing the multiplane approach possible within Gravity.jl. Finally, 18 additional spherical Jaffe profiles are used to describe 18 spectroscopically confirmed cluster galaxies identified from the MUSE data, including the BCG. For these galaxies, the central velocity dispersion $\sigma$ and truncation radius $r_{cut}$ are scaled according to the galaxy luminosity in the HST/F160W band assuming the following scaling relations:

$$ \displaystyle\sigma^{gal}=\sigma^{ref}\left(\frac{L_{gal}}{L_{ref}}\right)^{\alpha}, \displaystyle r^{gal}_{cut}=r^{ref}_{cut}\left(\frac{L_{gal}}{L_{ref}}\right)^{\beta}; $$

where $L_{gal}$ is the F200W luminosity of the cluster member. In the model we assume $\alpha=0.25$ and $\beta=0.50$ , which is equivalent to assuming a constant mass-to-light ratio across the cluster population (Bergamini et al., 2019; Oguri, 2010, see), and thus our only free parameters for the cluster members’ modeling are $\sigma^{ref}$ and $r^{ref}_{cut}$ .

To constrain the lens model with the data we adopt a parametric extended modeling approach. In addition to modeling the lens, we also model the brightness distribution of the multiply-imaged source (that is, MRG-M0150) using a Sérsic profile: this adds as free parameters the coordinates, the effective radius, total flux, the ellipticity and the position angle of the source.

In total the model contains 21 free parameters and is constrained by 22781 pixels. The model is optimized to reproduce the observed multiple images of the source; our goodness-of-fit estimation is given by the residuals between the model-predicted and observed shape of the multiple images. To sample the full parameter space of the models employed in this work, we carry out the Gravity.jl fits using a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm to obtain posterior distributions.

## Appendix B Kinematic modeling with MOKA3D

We perform 3D kinematics fitting of the ionized gas emission in MRG-M0150 using the de-lensed maps of ionized gas surface brightness in the source plane, along with the line profiles in each spaxel, in order to to reconstruct the geometry and velocity structure of the outflow. The MOKA3D code requires the observations’ grid to be regularly sampled and to convolve the model with the PSF of the instrument. Since we have to work on the source plane, we need to deal with the distortion of the NIRSpec/IFU spaxels and PSF caused by the application of the lens model, and to make them suitable to be fed to MOKA3D. We resample the source-plane cubes onto a regular grid of pixels with area much smaller than the minimum size of the original pixels in the following way: we first construct the regular grid, then for each of the original pixels we assign the surface signal and noise values to the closest pixel in the new grid, and put NaN values elsewhere. MOKA3D performs a convolution of the model with the PSF of the instrument; in this way we can ignore any correlated noise deriving from the resampling as long as the PSF convolution is applied, since the dimension of the PSF is much greater than the pixels in the new grid. In order to obtain the PSF on the source plane, we apply the same lens model to the instrumental PSF of NIRSpec/IFU. The 2D PSF of NIRSpec/IFU is first positioned to overlap the centroid of the galaxy in the image plane and then de-lensed onto the source plane.

We verify that the magnification does not vary greatly across the analyzed spaxels (as visible in Fig.12), and thus we should be able to apply the “centrally de-lensed” PSF across the entire cube. However, spaxels belonging to the bin that is closer to the critical line are experiencing higher levels of magnification than the rest of the galaxy ( $\mu\sim 12$ instead of $\mu\sim 4$ ): applying the same "centrally de-lensed" PSF to these spaxels may not be accurate, and may affect the resulting 3D reconstruction of the outflow by the fitting code. To verify that this is not the case, we show in Fig. 13 the shape of NIRSpec/IFU’s PSF overlapped onto the galaxy’s centroid in the image plane (upper left) and how that gets distorted when projecting it onto the source plane (upper right). In the central row of panels we verify that changing the PSF position away from the galaxy centroid in the image plane (left) results in a source-plane PSF that does not differ significantly from the centrally de-lensed one. Fitting both source-plane PSFs with an anisotropic 2D Gaussian model, we find only a small variation of the FWHM of the dislocated PSF’s of 8% along the minor axis and 0.2% along the major axis with respect to the centrally-located one. However, when positioning the PSF onto spaxels nearing the critical line in the image plane (last row), the magnification jumps to 3x the median value elsewhere and the PSF gets highly distorted along a preferential axis, with a variation in FWHM of 60% along the minor axis and 7% along the major one with respect to the center. Nonetheless, spaxels affected by the higher magnification form a small minority of all the spaxels analyzed, on top of being lower in signal-to-noise with respect to the central parts of the galaxy (see Fig.1). For this reason, the spatial bins are large near the critical line, and convolution by the PSF has only a very small effect. Thus, we decide to apply the centrally-projected de-lensed PSF to the entire resampled and de-lensed cubes to be fitted with MOKA3D, neglecting any change in magnification levels. The fact that we get consistent results from the MOKA3D fitting of the ${\rm H\alpha}$ emission – detected in all the analyzed bins – and the [OIII] line – which is not detected in the external parts of the galaxy, thus the fit does not include any of the greatly magnified spaxels – is evidence that our central PSF approximation is not significantly affecting the 3D kinematics fitting results.

## Abstract

We present the stellar metallicities and multi-element abundances (C, Mg, Si, Ca, Ti, Cr, and Fe) of 15 massive (log $M/M_{\odot}=10.2-11.2$ ) quiescent galaxies at $z=1-3$ , derived from ultradeep JWST-SUSPENSE spectra. Compared to quiescent galaxies at $z\sim 0$ , these galaxies exhibit a deficiency of 0.26 $\pm 0.04$ dex in [C/H], 0.16 $\pm 0.03$ dex in [Fe/H], and 0.07 $\pm 0.04$ dex in [Mg/H], implying rapid formation and quenching before significant enrichment from asymptotic giant branch stars and Type Ia supernovae. Additionally, we find that galaxies forming at higher redshift consistently show higher [Mg/Fe] and lower [Fe/H] and [Mg/H], regardless of their observed redshift. The evolution in [Fe/H] and [C/H] is therefore primarily driven by lower-redshift samples naturally including galaxies with longer star-formation timescales. In contrast, the lower [Mg/H] likely reflects earlier-forming galaxies expelling larger gas reservoirs during their quenching phase. Consequently, the mass-metallicity relation, primarily reflecting [Mg/H], is somewhat lower at $z=1-3$ compared to the lower redshift relation. Finally, we compare our results to standard stellar population modeling approaches employing solar abundance patterns and non-parametric star-formation histories (using Prospector). Our SSP-equivalent ages agree with the mass-weighted ages from Prospector, while the metallicities disagree significantly. Nonetheless, the metallicities better reflect [Fe/H] than total [Z/H]. We also find that star-formation timescales inferred from elemental abundances are significantly shorter than those from Prospector, and we discuss the resulting implications for the early formation of massive galaxies.

#### Keywords:

## I Introduction

The chemical makeup of a galaxy is intimately linked to its past star formation, the amount of gas and stars it accretes, and the gas that is expelled through outflows. Consequently, the metal content of galaxies reflects fundamental physical processes that influence their evolution, such as star formation efficiency, feedback from massive stars and active galactic nuclei (AGN), and previous merger events. By characterizing how the metallicities of galaxies evolve across redshifts, we can obtain direct insights into the processes shaping galaxy growth throughout cosmic time.

In the nearby universe, galaxies display a tight correlation between their stellar mass and metallicity, known as the mass-metallicity relation [58, 90, 38, 47, MZR; e.g.,]. For star-forming galaxies, the gas-phase MZR has been routinely studied out to $z\sim 3$ mostly using strong-line indicators [62, 95, 77, 78, 72, 80, e.g.,] and has recently been confirmed up to $z\sim 8$ with the advent of JWST [54, 70, 28]. Quiescent galaxies, however, lack the strong emission lines needed for gas-phase measurements, so we instead rely on faint absorption lines originating from stellar atmospheres. At higher redshifts, measuring stellar metallicity becomes increasingly challenging as key absorption features shift to near-infrared (NIR) wavelengths, where ground-based spectroscopic observations are severely hindered by skylines. As a result, the MZR of quiescent galaxies has only been systematically studied up to $z\sim 0.7$ , showing little evolution since $z\sim 0$ [19, 37, 4, 8].

Beyond $z\sim 1$ , the picture is much less clear. Currently, there are only a handful of stellar metallicity measurements of quiescent galaxies at $z=1-2.2$ based on absorption lines, mostly relying on methods such as spectral stacking [71, 14], observations of rare lensed massive galaxies [43, 64, 96, 1, 42], low-resolution spectroscopy [67, 35, 1], or utilizing extreme integration times on the most efficient ground-based telescopes [49, 50, 51, 9]. Despite the small samples at these redshifts, there is a growing consensus that massive quiescent galaxies at $z\gtrsim 1$ exhibit significantly lower [Fe/H] compared to their present-day counterparts [50, 96, 9, e.g.,]. There are, however, a couple of conflicting findings, with two studies reporting exceptionally high metallicities comparable to the most metal-rich galaxies at $z\sim 0$ [60, 43]. These contrasting results may not be surprising, given that the uncertainties in individual measurements remain high, and the methods vary significantly between studies [60, 71, 49, 35, 79, e.g.,].

Understanding the metallicities of distant quiescent galaxies is crucial, as it holds significant implications for the enrichment, star-formation timescales, quenching, and assembly of galaxies across cosmic time. Specifically, the multi-element abundance patterns provide direct insight into the star-formation histories (SFHs) of galaxies. Such insight is largely owed to the diverse enrichment timescales of the elements. $\alpha$ elements (e.g., O and Mg) are instantaneously released by core-collapse supernovae (CC SNe). C and N are released approximately equally by CC SNe and by the winds of low-mass asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars which only contribute after a characteristic delay-time of $\sim 250$ Myr [27, 26, 61, 45, e.g.]. Fe-peak elements are enriched by both CC and the explosions of intermediate-mass stars (Type Ia SNe; Ia SNe), which occur only after a longer delay [65, of $\sim 1$ Gyr].

To fully exploit chemical compositions for understanding the formation histories of massive galaxies, we need a larger sample of massive quiescent galaxies at $z\gtrsim 1$ with deep spectra covering multiple absorption features. Such observations are now finally possible with JWST. To that end, we have conducted the JWST-SUSPENSE program, an ultradeep rest-frame optical spectroscopic NIRSpec/MSA survey of 20 massive quiescent galaxies at $z=1-3$ [81].

In this paper, we present the metallicities and multi-element abundances of distant quiescent galaxies at $z=1-3$ from the JWST-SUSPENSE survey. In Section II we describe the observations and elemental abundance analysis, in Section III we present the abundance results, in Section IV we present the MZR at $z=1-3$ , and in Section V we discuss the implications of the results on star-formation timescales, the assembly of massive galaxies, and star-formation quenching. In Section V we also compare the full-spectrum modeling results to those from Prospector and discuss the implications of this comparison on the early formation of massive galaxies. In Section VI, we present a summary. Throughout this Paper, we assume a Kroupa [52] IMF, solar abundances from Asplund [3], and a flat $\Lambda$ CDM cosmology with $\Omega_{m}=0.3$ and $H_{0}=70~\rm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ .

## II Observations & Analysis

All galaxies in this study are drawn from the JWST-SUSPENSE Program (ID:2110) which obtained ultra-deep (16.4 hr) NIRSpec-MSA/G140M-F100LP observations of a sample of 20 massive quiescent galaxies at $z=1-3$ [81]. The spectroscopic observations were reduced using a modified version of the JWST Science Calibration Pipeline [11] v1.12.5, and version 1183 of the Calibration Reference Data System (CRDS) [see 81, for details]. Primary targets were initially identified using the UltraVISTA K-band selected DR3 catalog [68] and selected to be quiescent using the $UVJ$ criterion from Muzzin et al. [69]. The targets represent the general population of quiescent galaxies at $z=1-3$ , encompassing the full quiescent range in $UVJ$ space at these redshifts, and are all confirmed to have quiescent stellar populations [81, see].

The observations cover wavelengths from $0.97$ to $1.84,\mu$ m, corresponding to a typical rest-frame range of approximately $3700$ to $7000$ Å. Most objects have coverage of the Mgb line, several prominent Fe features, and multiple Balmer lines. The stellar masses and star-formation rates were derived by Slob et al. [81] by fitting the spectra and photometry simultaneously with Prospector [55, 44] assuming a Chabrier [17] IMF. They consider two non-parametric SFH models; a fixed-bin model [55] and a post-starburst model [86]. For more details on target selection, observing strategy, data reduction, redshift determination, and stellar population properties we refer to Slob et al. [81].

We measure the individual elemental abundances and stellar population ages using a custom full-spectrum fitting code alf $\alpha$ [6]11 1 https://github.com/alizabeverage/alfalpha based on the alf fitting code presented in Conroy et al. [25]. The Conroy et al. [25] models were developed to measure the elemental abundance patterns of old ( $\gtrsim$ 1 Gyr) stellar populations. They combine metallicity-dependent MIST isochrones [20], empirical MILES and IRTF spectral libraries [76, 93], and synthetic metallicity- and age-dependent elemental response spectra for 19 elements.

The models assume a single burst of star formation and a Kroupa [52] IMF. We fit for a total of 20 free parameters; velocity offset, velocity dispersion, single SSP-equivalent stellar population age, isochrone metallicity, 10 individual elemental abundances (Fe, C, N, Mg, Na, Si, Ca, Ti, Cr), Balmer emission line flux, the emission line velocity and broadening, a shift in the effective temperature of the fiducial isochrones ( $T_{\rm eff}$ ), and an instrumental jitter term to account for under/overestimation of the uncertainties. The abundance ratios of the other nine elements are fixed to solar ([X/Fe] = 0) following results of the mock-recovery test presented in Beverage et al. [8]. We use the dynesty dynamic nested sampling package [82] to sample the posterior distributions of the 20 parameters.

Before fitting, we smooth the models to the instrumental resolution of the observations. We derive the instrumental resolution as a function of wavelength in the raw spectral frames using msafit [31]. We provide msafit with the morphology of each galaxy, its position and angle with respect to the MSA slit, and a spectrum filled with equally spaced delta functions that simulate idealized emission lines. The software then simulates a 2D spectrum for each object. We process these 2D spectra using the JWST NIRSpec reduction pipeline in the same manner as the actual data. Finally, we measure the spectral resolution by analyzing the broadening of the simulated emission lines. We find that the wavelength dependence of the instrumental resolution is consistent with the online pre-launch estimates from JDox, but typically a factor of 1.3 better, corresponding to a resolution of $R\sim 1300$ . For each galaxy, we derive this factor and assume the corrected JDox curve when fitting. See Slob et al. [81] for more details on this procedure.

During the fitting procedure, the spectral continuum is removed from the observations by fitting an $n=7$ Chebyshev polynomial to the ratio of the data to the model. We note that the results are robust to decisions regarding the order of the polynomial. Where available, we fit the wavelength regions $3800-4800$ Å, $4800-5800$ Å, $5800-6400$ Å, and $8000-8600$ Å (each with their own normalized continuum). We mask the NaD absorption feature, the [OIII] lines where present, and the H $\alpha$ +[NII] complex. We also exclude wavelengths $6400-8000$ Å due to the dominant TiO absorption in the spectrum, as these broad features are typically over-fitted by the continuum polynomial.

After fitting all 20 galaxies, we visually inspect the best-fit model, the normalizing polynomial, and the corresponding corner plots. We remove five galaxies; two because they have low S/N ( $<$ 15 per rest-frame Å; 130183, 130934), one because it is lacking wavelength coverage of key absorption features (130208), and two because of strong emission lines likely associated with AGN (130647, 128452). We also re-fit 127941, masking the H $\beta$ region, which was poorly fit due to spectral contamination. Object 127108 is also re-fit, masking the region $>5500\,$ Å due to the lack of clear features. Finally, for each object, we inspect the posteriors of all 10 fitted elements and determine which elements can be constrained by requiring their posterior to be Gaussian and not run against the prior limits ( $-$ 0.5 and 0.5 dex). Figure 1 shows the quiescent SUSPENSE spectra at $z=1-3$ and corresponding best-fit alf $\alpha$ models. We present the stellar population properties and elemental abundances [X/H] in Table 1. The elements flagged as “poorly constrained” during the visual inspection are omitted from Table 1. We also omit the abundances of 129966 because the best-fit age is below the lowest age in the stellar population models (1 Gyr). Tables of the elemental abundance ratios [X/Fe] and [X/Mg] are provided in Appendix A.

## III The multi-elemental abundances of distant quiescent galaxies

In this section, we present the multi-element abundances of the massive quiescent galaxies at $z=1-3$ from the JWST-SUSPENSE program. For each SUSPENSE galaxy, we only consider the elements that have well-behaved normal posterior distributions. Among the ten fitted elements, C, Mg, and Fe have the most galaxies with well-constrained measurements, likely due to their prominent absorption features, such as CH (G4300), Mgb, Fe5270, Fe5335, and Fe5406.

In Figure 2, we present the formation time ( $t_{\mathrm{form}}$ ), [Fe/H], [Mg/H], [Fe/Mg], and [C/Mg] as a function of line-of-sight velocity dispersion (circles). Here, we adopt Mg as the reference element instead of Fe (i.e., [X/Mg]) because it is mostly produced by CC SNe and thus a simpler tracer of chemical enrichment [94, see e.g.,]. The formation time is calculated using the stellar ages from Table 1, corrected for the age of the universe at the observed redshift. The points are colored by their spectroscopic redshifts. We also include the results of stacked quiescent galaxies at $z\sim 0$ from SDSS (red squares) and $z\sim 0.7$ from LEGA-C [8, pink triangles]. The stacked SDSS spectra and corresponding elemental abundance results were first presented in Conroy et al. [21] and later re-fit by Beverage et al. [8] to reflect updates in the stellar population models [25, see]. We note that the SDSS fiber and the LEGA-C and SUSPENSE slits all cover similar physical radii (3 – 4 kpc). However, since galaxies were smaller in the past, the SUSPENSE and LEGA-C slits cover 1 – 1.2 $R_{e}$ , while SDSS covers only 0.4 – 0.8 $R_{e}$ .

In Figure 2, we also include all available elemental abundance measurements in the literature at $z=1-3$ . We only include measurements that use the same full-spectrum fitting method, and thus are comparable to the SUSPENSE results. We do not include grism or prism results because they rely heavily on the shape of the continuum and are therefore highly susceptible to fitting degeneracies. We also exclude abundances derived from Lick indices because, at these redshifts, the individual absorption features are faint and easily contaminated by NIR skylines. We color all points by their spectroscopic redshifts.

In each panel of Figure 2, we present the results from a linear structural regression fit applied to all available points within the redshift range $z=1-3$ . The linear model assumes intrinsic scatter around the best-fit line, which is described by a third parameter alongside the slope and intercept. Using a Bayesian approach, we determine the best-fit line and its associated shaded confidence intervals by sampling the posterior distributions with MCMC. We fit two relations to the formation times, one at $z<1.7$ (light blue) and another at $z>1.7$ (dark blue). During the fitting process, we set a lower limit of 0.1 dex on the uncertainties of the elemental abundance, to prevent single high S/N measurements from dominating the fit and to account for possible systematic uncertainties.

In the top left panel of Figure 2, we find that the formation redshifts of the SUSPENSE galaxies range from $z_{\rm form}=1.5$ to $9$ . No clear trends are observed between $\sigma$ and formation time at $z\gtrsim 1$ . However, there is a clear trend with observed redshift, where typical galaxies at $z\gtrsim 1$ formed earlier than those at lower redshifts, as expected. This redshift trend is also evident within the $z\gtrsim 1$ sample, with the best-fit relation for $z>1.7$ being lower than that for $z<1.7$ . A similar trend has been shown by Beverage et al. [8] and will be discussed in detail in Section V.2

In the next panel, we show that quiescent galaxies at $z=1-3$ have [Fe/H] ranging from $-$ 0.6 to 0.3, with typical values of $-$ 0.22. We find a trend between $\sigma$ and [Fe/H], with a statistically significant slope (2 $\sigma$ certainty). The normalization of these measurements are 0.16 $\pm 0.03$ dex lower than what is found at $z\sim 0$ and $z\sim 0.7$ . A 1D Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test comparing the Fe abundances of galaxies at $z\sim 0$ and $z\sim 2$ yields significant p-values ( $<0.01$ ), allowing us to reject the null hypothesis and conclude that the Fe abundances of these two populations are drawn from different distributions. Thus, we confirm earlier results that quiescent galaxies at $z\sim 2$ are Fe-deficient [49, 50, 67, 96, 9, 42]. In the next panel, we find that [Mg/H] varies from $-$ 0.3 to 0.6, with a typical value of [Mg/H] $=0.15$ . The slope of the $\sigma-$ [Mg/H] relation agrees with the results at $z\sim 0$ and $z\sim 0.7$ and the normalization is only slightly lower (0.07 $\pm 0.04$ dex).

*Figure 4: [Fe/H], [Mg/H], and [Mg/Fe] as a function of galaxy formation time for massive quiescent galaxies at $z=0-3$ . Data points for the redshift range $z=1-3$ are color-coded based on their spectroscopic redshift, and their shapes follow the same legend as Figure 2. The red circles [pink triangles] represent individual quiescent galaxies from SDSS [LEGA-C] [96, 8]. Typical uncertainties for the SDSS and LEGA-C points are shown in the bottom right of each panel. In the bottom left panel of Figure 2 we find [Fe/Mg] ranging from $-0.50$ to $-$ 0.10, with a typical value of $-$ 0.35. The best-fit $\sigma$ -[Fe/Mg] relation has a negative slope, in agreement with lower redshift results, however, the relation is offset to lower [Fe/Mg] by 0.10 $\pm 0.04$ dex. A 1D KS test of [Fe/Mg] show that the $z\sim 0$ and $z\sim 2$ abundances are drawn from different distributions, with a mildly significant p-value ( $<0.05$ ). This low [Fe/Mg] is consistent with the other results at similar redshifts in this figure [49, 9, 43, 42].

In the bottom right panel, we show [C/Mg]. We highlight that these are the first measurements of C abundances for a sample of distant quiescent galaxies and that only one other [C/Mg] measurement at these redshifts is available in the literature [43]. We find [C/Mg] ranges from $-0.55$ to $-0.05$ , with a typical value of $-0.3$ , in good agreement with Jafariyazani et al. [43]. The best-fit trend with $\sigma$ is still highly uncertain given that there are only 10 C measurements at this redshift but it is clear that the SUSPENSE galaxies have $\sim 0.2$ dex lower [C/Mg] than the $z\sim 0$ and $z\sim 0.7$ samples (3 $\sigma$ certainty). Given that the average [Mg/H] is similar (to within 0.07 dex) across the redshift samples, the low [C/Mg] and [Fe/Mg] are caused by deficiencies in C and Fe.

Next, we present the elemental abundance patterns of the SUSPENSE galaxies in Figure 3. We show the average absolute abundances [X/H] (top panel) the abundance ratios with respect to Fe [X/Fe], (middle panel), and the abundance ratios with respect to Mg [X/Mg] (bottom panel). We only include elements for which we have at least five constrained individual measurements; namely C, Mg, Si, Ca, Ti, and Cr, and Fe. The small blue squares represent the individual abundances from SUSPENSE, while the large squares depict the mean of these measurements. The black error bars are calculated by perturbing the abundances of each data point based on their uncertainties and then determining the standard deviation of the resulting mean abundance values. Figure 3 also includes the abundance patterns of $z\sim 0$ (red circles) and $z\sim 0.7$ quiescent galaxies (pink triangles) from Beverage et al. [8]. These $z\sim 0$ [ $z\sim 0.7$ ] results represent the average of thousands [hundreds] of quiescent galaxies from the same velocity dispersion range as the SUSPENSE galaxies (200 – 300 km -1).

Consistent with the findings of Figure 2, massive quiescent galaxies at all three redshift intervals have non-solar abundance patterns, being deficient with respect to Mg. These trends are further evident when examining the individual elements in greater detail. In the top panel of Figure 3, we find that distant quiescent galaxies in SUSPENSE have significantly lower [C/H] and [Fe/H] ( $>3\sigma$ certainty) and slightly lower [Mg/H] (1.5 $\sigma$ ) than the $z<1$ galaxies. Specifically, [C/H], [Fe/H], and [Mg/H] are lower by 0.25, 0.16, and 0.07 dex, respectively, than at $z\sim 0$ . Therefore, the [Mg/Fe] enhancement observed in the central panel is primarily driven by a deficiency in Fe. Moving on to the other elements, we find that Ca has a similar behavior as Mg, with a mostly constant [Ca/H] across the three redshift regimes, but with enhanced [Ca/Fe] and [Ca/Mg] at higher redshift. Ti is unique because the absolute abundance [Ti/H] and abundance ratios [Ti/Fe] and [Ti/Mg] increase with increasing redshift. We highlight that high Ti abundances present a long-standing problem in chemical evolution modeling [48, e.g.,]. [Cr/H] on the other hand behaves more like Fe and C, with [Cr/H] being lower at $z=1-3$ . This result is unsurprising given that Cr is typically considered an Fe-peak element. Si shows no significant evolution in [X/H], [X/Fe], or [X/Mg]. Thus, Si behaves more similarly to Mg and Ca. However, the abundance uncertainties on Ti, Si, and Cr are quite large. We note that these abundance results are roughly consistent with the only other existing abundance pattern at $z\gtrsim 0.7$ , observed in a lensed quiescent galaxy by Jafariyazani et al. [43]. In Section V.1, we explore the implications of these abundance patterns in the context of chemical enrichment histories.

Finally, in Figure 4, we show [Fe/H], [Mg/H], and [Mg/Fe] as a function of formation time, as in Zhuang et al. [96]. In addition to the SUSPENSE sample (blue circles, colored by spectroscopic redshift), we include individual results from massive quiescent galaxies in the SDSS survey from Zhuang et al. [96, red circles] and LEGA-C from Beverage et al. [8, pink triangles]. In each panel of Figure 4, we remove the first-order dependence on stellar mass by subtracting the SDSS $M_{*}-$ abundance relations from Zhuang et al. [96] from all galaxies and then scaling them to the value of the $M_{*}-$ abundance relations at $M_{*}=10^{11}\;M_{\odot}$ . We utilize the Pearson correlation coefficient to assess the degree of correlation between the parameters in Figure 4. We include all points in Figure 4 (at all redshifts) when computing the degree of correlation. The resulting Pearson coefficients and corresponding $p$ -values are listed in the top left of each panel. Correlations with $p$ -values $p<0.01$ are considered significant.

At fixed stellar mass, the formation time and [Fe/H] have a significant positive correlation ( $r=0.59$ ), with galaxies forming at earlier times having lower Fe enrichment. [Mg/H] shows a moderate positive correlation ( $r=0.30$ ), with galaxies forming earlier having slightly lower Mg enrichment. Finally, there is a negative correlation ( $r=-0.40$ ) between [Mg/Fe] and formation time, indicating galaxies that form earlier have slightly higher [Mg/Fe]. These correlations are primarily driven by the large quantity and dynamic range in $t_{\mathrm{form}}$ of $z\sim 0$ abundance measurements and thus agree with the results presented in Zhuang et al. [96]. Therefore, it is striking that the correlations found at lower redshifts are mostly consistent with the $z\sim 2$ data, in the sense that the oldest galaxies at $z\sim 0$ have similar abundance patterns as those at $z\sim 2$ . In Section V.2, we discuss the implications of these results on the assembly of massive galaxies.

## IV The Stellar Mass-Metallicity Relation at $z\sim 2$

In this section, we present the stellar mass-metallicity relation of quiescent galaxies at $z=1-3$ . In Figure 5, we show the stellar metallicities $\log\left(Z/Z_{\odot}\right)$ of the JWST-SUSPENSE quiescent galaxies as a function of their stellar mass (circles). We compute these metallicities following the calibration $\log\left(Z/Z_{\odot}\right)=$ [Fe/H] $+0.94$ [Mg/Fe] from Thomas et al. [89]. As in Figure 2, we include all existing measurements of stellar metallicities derived from full-spectrum fitting at $z=1-3$ derived using the same full-spectrum fitting method and underlying models. For comparison, we also include the $z\sim 0$ MZR and corresponding 1 $\sigma$ scatter from Gallazzi et al. [38, black line and gray shaded region]. Additionally, we show individual measurements for a subsample of these SDSS galaxies from Zhuang et al. [96, gray hexagons]. The Gallazzi et al. [38] relation was measured using a different method than Zhuang et al. [96], with different stellar population models, and assuming a different solar abundance pattern. Therefore, we calibrate the Gallazzi et al. [38] MZR to match the normalization of the Zhuang et al. [96] measurements by applying a shift of +0.16 dex.

We fit a mass-metallicity relation to all available $z=1-3$ measurements using the same structural linear regression applied to the abundances in Figure 2, where we assume that the points have an intrinsic scatter around the best-fit line. Again, we set the lower limit on the error of the metallicity to 0.1 dex so that high S/N measurements do not dominate the fit. Uncertainties on all stellar mass estimates are assumed to be 0.1 dex, to properly account for systematic uncertainties involved in the stellar population modeling [see 49, for motivation of mass uncertainties]. The best-fit parameters and corresponding uncertainties are estimated using MCMC. We use the same fitting method to re-determine the MZR at $z\sim 0$ (red line) and $z\sim 0.7$ (pink line) for the Zhuang et al. [96] and Beverage et al. [8] samples, respectively. We emphasize again that the individual metallicity measurements at $z\sim 0$ and $z\sim 0.7$ were made using the same full-spectrum modeling method as the $z=1-3$ sample.

The best-fit stellar MZRs at each redshift interval correspond to the following relations:

$z=1-3:$

$$ \log\left(Z/Z_{\odot}\right)=0.19_{-0.12}^{+0.17}\;\log\left(\frac{M_{*}}{10^{11}\,M_{\odot}}\right)+0.13_{-0.11}^{+0.05} $$

$z\sim 0.7:$

$$ \log\left(Z/Z_{\odot}\right)=0.08_{-0.04}^{+0.04}\;\log\left(\frac{M_{*}}{10^{11}\,M_{\odot}}\right)+0.21_{-0.02}^{+0.02} $$

$z\sim 0:$

$$ \log\left(Z/Z_{\odot}\right)=0.27_{-0.02}^{+0.02}\;\log\left(\frac{M_{*}}{10^{11}\,M_{\odot}}\right)+0.30_{-0.02}^{+0.02} $$

The slope of the MZR at $z=1-3$ is consistent with that at $z\sim 0$ , within the uncertainties. The normalization, though, appears to have increased by $0.17\pm 0.09$ since $z\sim 2$ . We note that the sample at $z=1-3$ is still small, and the metallicity measurements have significant statistical uncertainties. Consequently, the evidence for evolution remains below the $2\sigma$ level. Thus, larger samples and deeper observations are needed to confirm this potential evolution with more certainty.

An evolving MZR, if confirmed, is not surprising given that the total metal content of a galaxy is primarily in $\alpha$ elements (70 percent22 2 Calculated using the Asplund [3] solar abundances and taking $\alpha$ elements to include N, O, Mg, Na, Ne, S, Si, Ti, and Ca. by mass) and that we find slightly lower Mg in Figure 3. Even though distant quiescent galaxies are Fe deficient, Fe-peak elements only contribute 10 percent by mass to the total metallicity. Therefore, the observed offset in the MZR to lower $Z/Z_{\odot}$ could be explained by these galaxies having lower Mg abundances.

Other studies based on Lick indices instead point to a redshift-invariant MZR, with galaxies at $z\sim 2$ having super-solar $Z_{*}$ [60, 71]. However, these conclusions are based on individual measurements or a single stacked spectrum, and therefore they carry large uncertainties. Similarly, Estrada-Carpenter et al. [35] report a redshift-invariant MZR, with stellar metallicities derived from low-resolution spectroscopy. In section V.4, we compare these methods and demonstrate that metallicities derived from spectrophotometric fitting primarily reflect [Fe/H]. Given the Fe deficiencies found in this work, it is notable that Estrada-Carpenter et al. [35] find no evolution in the MZR.

## V Discussion & Implications

### V.1 Star-formation timescales

In this work, we present the first abundance pattern study (including Fe, C, Mg, Si, Ca, Ti) based on a sample of $z>1$ quiescent galaxies. Jafariyazani et al. [43] had previously measured an abundance pattern at $z\sim 2$ , but only for a single lensed system, whereas Beverage et al. [9] measured only the Mg and Fe abundances of a larger sample of quiescent galaxies at $z\sim 1.4$ and $z\sim 2.1$ . In this section, we discuss the implication of multi-element abundance results on the star-formation histories of distant quiescent galaxies.

A key observation from Figure 3 was that massive queiscent galaxies at $z=1-3$ are deficient in Fe and C, whereas Mg, Si, Ca, and Ti have higher abundances. When considering the full ISM enrichment over a stellar population’s lifetime, Fe is forged approximately equally in CC and SNe Ia, whereas C is enriched approximately equally by CC SNe and low-mass AGB stars. The other elements, Mg, Si, Ca, and Ti, are all primarily $\alpha$ elements, produced in CC SNe. These processes enrich over a diverse set of timescales; exploding massive stars (CC SNe) eject $\alpha$ elements almost instantaneously after the commencement of star formation, swiftly incorporating them into subsequent stellar generations. Alternatively, low- to intermediate-mass stars enrich the ISM on a delayed timescale due to their longer lifespans. One mechanism is via SNe Ia, which typically eject Fe-peak elements (e.g., Cr and Fe) only after a time delay of $\sim 0.5-1$ Gyr. The other mechanism is via AGB stars, which have even shorter delay times than SNe Ia, enriching primarily C (and N) as early as 50 Myr but with a typical delay of $\sim 250$ Myr [27, 26, 61, 45, e.g.,]. Thus, galaxies that stop forming stars before significant AGB and SNe Ia contributions have very low Fe-peak and C $+$ N stellar abundances, but still high $\alpha$ abundances.

Considering the different enrichment timescales, our low C and Fe abundance results imply that the SUSPENSE galaxies formed most of their stellar mass before significant AGB and Ia SNe enrichment, corresponding to a timescale of $\lesssim 0.2$ Gyr. Such an extreme star-formation timescale would translate to an SFR of $\geq 500~M_{\odot}\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$ , putting these galaxies among the most vigorous star-forming galaxies in the Universe [75, 33, 41, 59, e.g.,].

This interpretation assumes that the observed deficiencies in C and Fe are solely driven by shorter star-formation timescales in higher-redshift galaxies. However, variations in the IMF may also play a significant role in shaping the relative elemental abundances. For instance, a top-heavy IMF would increase the relative number of CC to Ia supernovae, increasing the Mg producers over the Fe producers. This would elevate [Mg/Fe] without requiring extremely short star-formation timescales [66, 88, e.g.,]. Furthermore, a top-heavy IMF could alter the IMF-averaged CC SNe yields, introducing even more variation. A top-heavy IMF is indeed plausible in these extreme galaxies, potentially due to unique environmental conditions or the effect of an integrated galaxy-wide IMF [36, e.g.,]. However, the extent of this impact—particularly on elements that are produced by multiple enrichment pathways—remains unclear. Detailed chemical evolution modeling is necessary to disentangle the respective roles of the IMF and star-formation timescales in producing these unusual abundance patterns.

Such detailed chemical evolution models would also provide more precise estimates of star-formation timescales, a task we leave for a future work. However, we note that the inferred extreme star-formation timescales conflict with the results from spectrophotometric fitting using the non-parametric star-formation histories of the SUSPENSE galaxies Slob et al. [81]. In Sections V.4 and V.5 we discuss the implications of these differences.

### V.2 The assembly of massive galaxies over cosmic time

Our elemental abundance patterns imply that galaxies at $z\sim 2$ on average formed earlier (Section III) and over shorter timescales (Section V.1) compared to galaxies with similar velocity dispersions at $z\sim 0$ and $z\sim 0.7$ . The most straightforward explanation for this observed increase is that galaxies in the quiescent sample at $z=1-3$ are among the earliest quenchers in the $z\sim 0$ population; galaxies that form over longer timescales quench and join the quiescent galaxy population at later times. Thus, by $z=0$ , the SUSPENSE sample represents only the extreme tail of the $t_{\mathrm{form}}$ distribution. This explanation is akin to the “progenitor bias” scenario [91, i.e.,] used, for example, to explain the size growth of quiescent galaxies over time [46, 92, 16, 74, e.g.,].

This progenitor bias scenario is reinforced by Figure 4, where we find a negative correlation between formation time and [Mg/Fe], irrespective of the observed redshift of the galaxies. Thus, the evolution in C and Fe is mostly due to the lower redshift samples naturally including galaxies with earlier formation times and shorter star-formation timescales.

A closer look at Figure 4, however, reveals that progenitor bias alone may not be able to explain the observations. If the $z\sim 2$ galaxies passively evolve over the past 10 billion years, without merging or experiencing late-time star formation, then the trends with formation time at $z\sim 0$ and $z\sim 2$ should exactly overlap at the earliest epochs. Instead, we find very few SDSS galaxies at these early formation times and we find that the $z\sim 2$ samples exhibit slightly lower [Fe/H] and [Mg/H], and higher [Mg/Fe] than the lower redshift samples. This offset was first identified by Zhuang et al. [96] using a small sample of objects at $z=1-3$ , and later confirmed by Beverage et al. [9] with a larger sample.
