Figure 4 shows the influence of light-weighting for two example SFH models. We consider models with a quickly declining SFH ( $\tau_{2}=4$ Gyr, shown in blue) and a slowly declining SFH ( $\tau_{2}=12$ Gyr, shown in orange) for fixed $\tau_{1}=1$ Gyr, $\tau_{*}=1$ Gyr, and $\eta=0.3$ . The normalized SFR in Figure 4a gives the fraction of the galaxy’s stellar mass formed per Gyr. A galaxy with a quickly declining SFH forms most of its stars early on, while a galaxy with a slowly declining SFH forms stars more steadily over time. As a result, the stellar ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ at the time of observation is younger for galaxies with a slowly declining SFH versus a quickly declining SFH, as shown by the difference between the blue and orange dashed curves in Figure 4b. Light-weighting, represented by the solid curves, gives more weight to younger stars, lowering the ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ for both models by a couple of Gyr at late times, with deviations from the mass-weighted ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ rapidly increasing at times close to $t_{\mathrm{obs}}$ .

Figures 4c and 4e show the evolution of gas-phase $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]$ and $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]$ for each model. $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]$ initially increases over time as Mg is produced by CCSN, then plateaus as the production of Mg reaches an equilibrium with the removal of Mg by stellar lockup and outflows. $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]$ starts out at the CCSN yield ratio, here $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}=0.45$ , then decreases as SNIa begin contributing Fe. $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]$ is lower for a galaxy with a rapidly declining SFR because the ratio of CCSN to delayed SNIa is lower at late times. Figures 4d and 4f show the corresponding mean stellar quantities, which have smaller differences between models. Light-weighting has minimal impact on ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ because the gas-phase $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]$ is flat at late times. However, light-weighting results in lower ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ at late times because it gives higher weight to the populations formed with the lowest $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]$ . Figures 4g and 4h plot ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ and ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ versus ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ . Somewhat coincidentally, the impact of light-weighting on ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ and on ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ nearly cancels, so mass-weighted and light-weighted tracks are nearly identical.

Figure 8 shows the influence of SFE and outflows on the mean abundance evolution for models with the reference SFH (solid orange curves in Figure 6a and 6b). Reducing (increasing) $\tau_{*}$ raises (lowers) ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ at early times and thus in galaxies with high ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ caused by early truncation of star formation. Conversely, reducing (increasing) $\eta$ raises (lowers) ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ at late times and thus in galaxies with younger ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ , while having little impact at early times. This behavior is consistent with our previous discussion: high SFE (short $\tau_{*}$ ) leads to more rapid growth of metallicity, but the late time equilibrium is governed by the degree of metal loss in outflows. In contrast to ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ , the influence of $\tau_{*}$ and $\eta$ on the ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ - $t_{\rm cut}$ and ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ - ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ trajectories is barely discernible. With these quantities specified, the prediction of ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ vs. ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ is remarkably robust within our family of models, with little sensitivity to the SFH parameters (Figure 6) and even less to $\tau_{*}$ and $\eta$ .

Increasing $t_{\rm start}$ reduces the ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ of the oldest galaxies, as there is less time for enrichment. For the $z=0$ galaxies, changing $t_{\rm start}$ from 0.5 Gyr to 1 Gyr is qualitatively similar to extending the rise time $\tau_{1}$ from 2 Gyr to 4 Gyr. However, for the $z=0.7$ galaxies the longer rise time produces a minimal change in ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ at a given ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ while shifting $t_{\rm start}$ has a substantial impact.

## IV Modeling observed elliptical populations

### IV.1 Representative Models

We use our results from Figure 11 to select representative models that reproduce the observed ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ and ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ of low, medium, and high velocity dispersion galaxies at $z=0$ and galaxies at $z=0.7$ . These models are described by star formation histories with rising timescales of $\tau_{1}=2$ and 4 Gyr, declining timescales of $\tau_{2}=8$ and 12 Gyr, and a star formation start time of $t_{\rm start}=0.5$ Gyr. The parameter that has the strongest impact on ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ is $t_{\rm cut}$ , the time at which star formation rapidly truncates. Figure 12 illustrates the relationship between $t_{\rm cut}$ and the predicted ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ for the representative models (see Figure 13) at $z=0$ and $z=0.7$ . The $z=0.7$ models display nearly identical tracks in ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ - $t_{\rm cut}$ . However, there are differences as large as $\sim 1$ Gyr in ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ between the $z=0$ models for a given $t_{\rm cut}$ when $t_{\rm cut}\gtrsim 4.5$ Gyr. Here, models having a higher star formation rate at late times (longer $\tau_{1}$ and/or longer $\tau_{2}$ ) have younger ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ at fixed $t_{\rm cut}$ . The horizontal lines mark the observed ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ for the lowest (youngest) and highest (oldest) velocity dispersion bins at each redshift (see Figure 13). The intersections of the horizontal lines and model curves indicate the truncation time required for each model to obtain the observed ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ . More massive, high- $\sigma$ ellipticals are older than less massive, low- $\sigma$ ellipticals and therefore cease star formation at an earlier $t_{\rm cut}$ .

Figure 13 compares our representative models to the observed ages and abundances of galaxies stacked in bins of velocity dispersion, $\sigma$ . Figure 11 shows that once the yields are fixed, there is not much leverage to boost ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ . With empirical yields described in Section III.2, there are no combinations of $\tau_{1}$ , $\tau_{2}$ , $\tau_{*}$ , and $\eta$ that can reproduce the observations. Because our models generally underproduce the observed ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ , we adopt $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}=0.55$ as our reference value in this section rather than 0.45 as in Section III. The dotted gray curves in Figure 13 show the reference model that is the central curve from Figure 11; the most important difference from the models in this section is the lower $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}=0.45$ .

Figure 13 demonstrates the difficulty of reproducing observed abundance trends in ellipticals with smooth star formation histories and yields that are empirically motivated by abundance trends in the Milky Way. Our reference model with $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}=0.45$ underpredicts the observed ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ values by $\sim 0.08$ dex at $z=0$ and $\sim 0.05$ dex at $z=0.7$ . For $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}=0.55$ , we find models that come close to the observed ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ - ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ and ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ - ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ trends at $z=0.7$ (blue and orange curves in panels c and d) and underpredict the observed ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ by $\sim 0.02-0.05$ dex for low- $\sigma$ ellipticals at $z=0$ (green curves in panels a and b). For the higher- $\sigma$ galaxies, achieving super-solar ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ at older ages requires higher SFE, which leads to a more rapid drop in ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ . For the mid- $\sigma$ galaxies, the gap between our representative model (pink curve) and the observed ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ is $\sim 0.06-0.08$ dex, and for the oldest, high- $\sigma$ ellipticals (blue curve) it is $\sim 0.07$ dex. We have made parameter choices that tend to maximize ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ at a given ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ subject to the constraints imposed by ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ , and one can see from Figure 11 that many alternative choices would worsen the agreement with the observed abundance trends.

Gaps of $\sim 0.05$ dex are small enough that they might be explained by systematic errors in the SSP fits themselves, e.g., because of imperfections in the stellar libraries used for the spectral synthesis. However, since we have already pushed our parameter choices to reduce discrepancies to this level, we will examine possible physical resolutions, arising from lower SNIa yields (Section IV.3) or from terminating bursts of star formation (Section IV.4). Even if systematic errors can adequately explain the gaps between our model predictions and the binned-average data, other mechanisms may be needed to explain individual galaxies that lie above the mean. Before considering these mechanisms, we re-examine the relationship between SSP fits and full evolutionary models, now guided by the models that come closest to matching the data. We return to a broader discussion of our results, including the choice of CCSN yields and the effects of the stellar IMF, in Section V.

Reducing $y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm Ia}$ by a factor of 1.65 is equivalent to reducing the normalization of the SNIa DTD in ellipticals by the same factor. However, observations suggest that the SNIa rate in galaxy clusters, which have a high fraction of elliptical and lenticular galaxies, is higher than the rate in star-forming field galaxies, not lower [43]. Because the stellar populations of ellipticals are old, observed rates probe the late phases of the delay time distribution, so this inference of a higher time-integrated rate depends on assuming that the DTD form is the same in cluster and field galaxies. It is also possible that the $y_{\mathrm{Fe}}^{\mathrm{Ia}}/y_{\mathrm{Fe}}^{\mathrm{cc}}$ in ellipticals is the same as that in our reference model, or higher, but that ellipticals preferentially lose SNIa products in galactic winds relative to CCSN products, even at epochs when they are actively forming stars and enriching their ISM. Such preferential ejection could arise if CCSN ejecta are trapped in dense star-forming gas while SNIa ejecta are released in lower-density gas that is more easily vented from the galaxy. Nonetheless, while these scenarios are possible, there seems to be no good empirical or theoretical argument for reduced $y_{\mathrm{Fe}}^{\mathrm{Ia}}/y_{\mathrm{Fe}}^{\mathrm{cc}}$ in elliptical galaxies other than the high ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ ratios.

[22] find that GCE models are more successful at reproducing Milky Way observations if the SNIa DTD has fewer short-delay supernovae than predicted by the $t^{-1.1}$ power-law advocated by, e.g., [43] and [81]. [61] argue that an exponential-like DTD fits observed SNIa rates as well as the power-law model (see also Palicio et al. 47). Dubay et al. show (in their Appendix B) that an exponential DTD with a timescale $\tau_{\rm Ia}\approx 1.5\,{\rm Gyr}$ is similar to the theoretically motivated single-degenerate DTD of [28], and a number of GCE studies have adopted this exponential form for the DTD (e.g., Schönrich and Binney 53, Andrews et al. 2; WAF). Relative to the $t^{-1.1}$ power-law with $t_{{\rm d,min}}=0.15\,{\rm Gyr}$ , the $\tau_{\rm Ia}=1.5\,{\rm Gyr}$ exponential DTD has a similar median delay time ( $\approx 1\,{\rm Gyr}$ ) but fewer SNIa at $t\ll 1\,{\rm Gyr}$ . The solid green curve in Figure 15 adopts the same parameters and $y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm Ia}$ as the blue curve but employs a single exponential DTD with $\tau_{\rm Ia}=1.5\,{\rm Gyr}$ . For the oldest ages, the predicted ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ is slightly higher than that of the reference model, which uses a sum of two exponentials to approximate a $t^{-1.1}$ power-law. However, at younger ages the predicted ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ is slightly lower because the exponential DTD has more intermediate-time SNIa than the long-tailed, power-law DTD. Thus, simply changing the form of the DTD to a single exponential does not improve agreement with the elliptical galaxy observations.

[22] also consider an exponential DTD with $\tau_{\rm Ia}=3\,{\rm Gyr}$ . We have repeated our calculations for this DTD (dotted green curve), and in this case, we get much better agreement with the data at $z=0.7$ and $z=0$ . Like the findings of [22], Figure 15 highlights the importance of pinning down both the form and the normalization of the SNIa DTD, and testing its universality across different types of galaxies.

### IV.4 Terminating Bursts of Star Formation

Our models assume flexible but smooth star formation histories. Bursts of star formation produce temporary boosts in [Mg/Fe] because the rate of $\alpha$ -element production from massive stars increases during the burst (WAF; Johnson and Weinberg 35). If a burst occurs at the beginning or middle of the SFH, then the Fe from SNIa progenitors formed in the burst will eventually be incorporated into stars, so we expect the impact on ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ to be small. A burst that terminates the galaxy’s SFH is different because the newly produced Mg can be incorporated into stars during the burst (self-enrichment), but the SNIa Fe production occurs after star formation has ceased. It has long been known that some galaxies, variously referred to as “E+A”, “K+A”, or “post-starburst”, undergo bursts of star formation before abruptly transitioning to quiescence [21, 85, 3, 42, 48]. However, it is unclear whether most early type galaxies end their SFH with a final burst.

To estimate the impact of a terminating burst, we compute the mean metallicity of stars formed in the burst using a “leaky box” chemical evolution model [31], which extends “closed box” evolution [65] by allowing outflow. We implicitly assume that the burst duration is long compared to the $\sim 30\,{\rm Myr}$ lifetime of massive stars, so that newly produced CCSN elements are incorporated into later generations within the burst, but short compared to the $\sim 1\,{\rm Gyr}$ timescale over which substantial SNIa Fe production would occur. A terminating burst could be triggered by a galaxy merger that brings a substantial amount of fresh gas, which dilutes the metallicity of the ISM but increases the fuel available to make stars. Our use of the leaky box model implies that any further gas accretion during the burst is negligible compared to the initial supply. While our calculation is idealized, it captures the distinctive ways that a terminating burst affects the mean stellar abundances of a galaxy and gives an approximate value of the quantitative impact on observables.

We give details of this calculation in Appendix B. The parameters of a burst in our model are $f_{g}$ , the ratio of gas remaining at the end of the burst to gas at the start of the burst, and $F_{D}$ , the ratio of accreted gas to gas present in the galaxy at the end of smooth evolution. For representative values of $f_{g}$ we consider $f_{g}=0.3$ and $f_{g}=0.05$ , corresponding to bursts that consume 70% and 95% of the initial gas supply. We assume that outflows during the burst are negligible, regardless of the value of $\eta$ assumed during smooth evolution. This choice maximizes the impact of the burst because all metals formed during the burst are retained.

For the dilution factor we consider $F_{D}=0$ , corresponding to a burst that only consumes the pre-existing gas in the ISM, and $F_{D}=3$ , corresponding to an accretion event that increases the gas supply by a factor $1+F_{D}=4$ . For example, $F_{D}=3$ could describe a galaxy with $10^{11}M_{\odot}$ of stars and $10^{10}M_{\odot}$ of remaining gas that accretes a gas rich companion with $3\times 10^{10}M_{\odot}$ of gas, triggering a burst. We ignore the impact of accreted stars. We assume that accretion lowers the ISM abundance of both Mg and Fe by a factor $(1+F_{D})$ , which is a reasonable approximation for a minor merger in which the accreted system has much lower metallicity than the main galaxy. The mass and abundances of stars formed during the burst are computed from Equation (B8) and Equation (B9), respectively.

The impact of a burst on observables is enhanced by light-weighting, as the stellar population formed during the burst is younger and brighter than the stellar populations formed during smooth evolution. We assume that the burst duration is long enough for self-enrichment but short compared to other GCE timescales. We therefore assign all stellar mass from the burst to the timestep ( $\Delta t=0.02\,{\rm Gyr}$ ) that immediately follows $t_{\rm burst}=t_{\rm cut}$ . Our procedure should be accurate for burst durations up to $\sim 0.3\,{\rm Gyr}$ , but for longer burst durations one could not ignore SNIa enrichment.

Models that convert a higher fraction of gas into stars during the burst ( $f_{g}=0.05$ ) produce more CCSN and therefore show a larger increase in $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]$ . If the ISM is diluted by pristine gas immediately before the burst ( $F_{D}=3$ ), then the $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]$ of burst stars is lower, and it even lies below the $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]$ at the end of the smooth evolution if only a small fraction of gas is converted into stars ( $f_{g}=0.3$ ).

We assume that the final bursts are long enough to incorporate CCSN products produced by stars formed in the burst, but short enough that there is no Fe enrichment from SNIa. As a result, all burst models increase $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]$ . Models with larger burst fractions show larger $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]$ increases, so in contrast to $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]$ the $F_{D}=3$ models have the largest boost of $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]$ . Figures 16d and 16f show the final light-weighted ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ and ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ of the entire galaxy. Relative to Figures 16c and 16e, abundance changes are reduced because the burst comprises only a fraction of the galaxy’s stars. Figures 16g and 16h plot ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ and ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ against ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ . Overall, adding a final burst of star formation increases ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ and decreases ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ , with both changes moving the models in the right direction to reproduce the observed data.

If self-enrichment during terminating bursts is indeed the explanation for the high observed ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ relative to our model predictions, it implies that these large final bursts of star formation are the norm in elliptical galaxy evolution, not the exception. Population synthesis models that isolate late star formation can test this conjecture. Furthermore, since not all galaxies will experience bursts of the same magnitude, we expect correlations between the fraction of stars formed immediately before quiescence and the mean abundances of the stellar population.

## V Discussion

### V.1 Yields and IMF

Our calculations show that the nucleosynthetic yields and SNIa DTD are the key factors governing the predicted ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ - ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ and ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ - ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ relations of ellipticals. Once we choose the yields and DTD, the SFH has only a small impact on the predicted relations (see Figures 6gh and 11), within the fairly wide range of behavior allowed by our smooth SFH parameters. The choices of SFE timescale $\tau_{*}$ and outflow efficiency $\eta$ have an important impact on the early and late evolution, respectively, of ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ , but they have limited impact on ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ (Figure 8). The high SFE needed to get early enrichment in ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ tends to drive down ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ , making it difficult to explain the high observed values of both quantities in the oldest, high- $\sigma$ ellipticals (Figure 11, Figure 13).

For our fiducial choice of yields, Equation 6, we are unable to reproduce the high observed ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ ratios in our $z\sim 0$ and $z\sim 0.7$ samples, falling short by 0.05-0.1 dex (dotted gray curve in Figure 13). As discussed in Section III, the overall normalization of these yields is motivated by the [50] determination of the mean Fe yield of CCSN; the ratio $y_{\rm Mg}^{\rm cc}/y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm cc}$ corresponding to $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}=0.45$ is motivated by the observed plateau in $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]$ for low metallicity stars in the Milky Way disk and halo; and the ratio $y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm Ia}/y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm cc}$ is motivated by the expectation that models evolve to $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]\approx 0$ at late times to explain solar abundances in MW disk stars.

Nearly all stars in APOGEE with $[{\rm Fe/H}]>-1.5$ have $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]<0.45$ (see Figure 1 of 80), and a plateau at $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}\leq 0.45$ is also supported by most of the data compiled by [37] (see their Figure 12) and by the Sgr dwarf and Milky Way halo stars shown by [55] (see their Figure 6). However, based on a sample of halo stars from the H3 survey extending to $[{\rm Fe/H}]=-3$ , [19] argue that the true core collapse plateau lies at $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}\approx 0.6$ , and that the roughly flat trend for stars with $-1.5\lesssim[{\rm Fe/H}]\lesssim-0.5$ already includes a substantial SNIa contribution (see also Maoz and Graur 43). With our higher choice of $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}=0.55$ , giving the yields in Equation 7, our smooth SFH models still underproduce the observed ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ , but at a level that is possibly within the systematic uncertainties of the SSP abundance measurements (Figure 13). Unfortunately, massive star and CCSN models are not robust enough to settle the choice of $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}$ theoretically, as illustrated by the fact that state-of-the-art models (e.g., Sukhbold et al. 62) miss the solar [O/Mg] ratio by 0.4 dex even though O and Mg are produced in stars of similar mass [29].

The empirical evidence for $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}\approx 0.45$ comes from stars with $[{\rm Fe/H}]<-0.5$ . Our models assume $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}$ is independent of metallicity, which is consistent with theoretical predictions (e.g., [46, 2]). However, these theoretical predictions could be incorrect, and the yield ratios at the $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\approx 0$ metallicities that matter most for our models could be higher than the plateau observed for lower metallicity stars.

Another possible explanation of the difference between our models and the data is that the IMF-averaged Mg and Fe yields in ellipticals are simply different than those in the Milky Way. For CCSN, the IMF-averaged yields could be different because of a difference in the high-mass slope of the IMF, perhaps connected to star formation in environments of high ambient pressure. A top-heavy IMF would increase the Mg and Fe yields $y_{\rm Mg}^{\rm cc}$ and $y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm cc}$ , making it easier to reproduce the observed ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ and ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ in the oldest galaxies and reducing the need for a high SFE to explain this rapid enrichment. Using the CCSN yields of [12], [30] find that changing the high-mass IMF slope from -2.3 [39] to -2.0 slightly decreases the predicted $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}$ , by 0.03 dex. We used VICE [35] to perform a similar calculation for yields from [62] with different choices of explosion landscape. Here we find that changing the high-mass IMF slope from -2.3 to -2.0 increases $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}$ , but only by 0.02-0.03 dex. Both of these calculations suggest that the IMF shape has little leverage on the CCSN Mg/Fe ratio. However, this dependence merits further investigation with other yield models.

Raising the CCSN yields relative to SNIa yields (higher $y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm cc}/y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm Ia}$ ) with a top-heavy IMF would help to boost ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ even if $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}$ is unchanged, similar to the effect shown in Figure 15. Black hole formation can also have a large impact on IMF-averaged yields (Griffith et al. 29; 80), even if the IMF itself is unchanged. However, while black hole formation may well depend on metallicity, there is no obvious reason it should be different in ellipticals vs. the Milky Way at a given metallicity.

Much of the discussion about IMF differences in ellipticals has focused on low-mass behavior, in particular on observations suggesting that high- $\sigma$ ellipticals have more low mass ( $M<0.5$ $M_{\odot}$ ) stars than predicted by a [39] IMF [73, 74, 17, 15]. Because these star have lifetimes longer than the age of the Universe, the main impact of increasing their relative numbers is to lower all yields — $y_{\rm Mg}^{\rm cc}$ , $y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm cc}$ , and $y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm Ia}$ — by the same factor. A bottom-heavy IMF thus makes it more difficult to explain rapid enrichment, but it probably has little impact on ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ predictions. If the increased numbers extend above the $\sim 1$ $M_{\odot}$ turnoff, then the SNIa rate could be boosted by increased white dwarf formation, possibly explaining the high SNIa rate inferred in galaxy clusters [43]. An increased $y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm Ia}/y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm cc}$ would worsen the discrepancy with observed ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ , opposite to the reduced $y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm Ia}/y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm cc}$ models considered in Section IV.3.

### V.2 Future Directions

Our results suggest several directions for future investigations. One is to fit model parameters directly to spectra instead of comparing the light-weighted ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ , ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ , ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ to SSP fit values. The tests presented in Figure 14 indicate that predicting SSP quantities is an effective shortcut, but the residual inaccuracies in this process may still be enough to affect the assessment of models. Fitting directly to observed spectra requires computing model spectra for continuous sequences of stellar populations as we have done in Figure 14, but this process could be made reasonably efficient. For a smooth SFH and $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}=0.45$ , we would not expect to obtain statistically acceptable fits to the data, since we cannot reproduce the observed ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ - ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ relation, but inspecting the discrepancies of best-fit models in spectral space might better reveal whether these discrepancies could arise from systematic uncertainties in the spectral modeling.

Another promising direction is to use broad-band SED measurements (photometry or spectrophotometry) in addition to the continuum-normalized absorption spectra modeled by alf. Codes such as Prospector [33] and BagPipes [10] use the broad-band SED to derive SFH constraints that go beyond effective population age defined by SSP fits. We might therefore hope to constrain our SFH parameters with the broad-band SED and allow absorption spectra to better constrain the yields and GCE parameters. In the context of ellipticals, it would be especially valuable to use the SED and spectra combination to probe the cessation of star formation and thus get insights into the physics of quenching. Our models assume a sharp cutoff at $t_{\rm cut}$ , but they allow an exponential decline before that, and the same ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ can be obtained with a rapid exponential decline and late cutoff or a slow decline and early cutoff. The predicted ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ - ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ tracks are surprisingly insensitive to the difference (Figure 6), but the combination with SED-fitting might distinguish such models. Most importantly, our modeling in Section IV.4 suggests that terminating bursts of star formation may play an important role in boosting ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ relative to the smooth-SFH predictions. Broad-band SED modeling may be able to confirm or refute the hypothesis that typical ellipticals terminate their star formation with a final burst.

The combined spectra-SED constraints become still more promising if they can be applied on a galaxy-by-galaxy basis in addition to the high-precision constraints for binned samples. Our preliminary investigations imply that galaxies at fixed $M_{\star}$ exhibit intrinsic scatter in SSP age, $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]$ , and $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]$ comparable to the statistical uncertainties for individual SDSS or LEGA-C spectra (A. Beverage et al., in preparation). If terminating bursts are a common phenomenon, we expect correlations between deviations from the mean $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]$ and the fraction of stars formed at the end of the galaxy’s SFH, as illustrated in Figure 18. The correlation of scatter in age, $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]$ , and $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]$ at fixed $M_{\star}$ or $\sigma$ can provide further insights into the termination of star formation and the factors that govern abundance ratios.

HST and JWST studies show that there are already substantial populations of quiescent galaxies present at $z=1-5$ . The combination of ground-based and JWST spectroscopy allows the first assessments of stellar metallicities and $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]$ ratios in such systems [6, 7, 38, 56, 9, e.g.,]. For massive star-forming galaxies, one can combine stellar $[{\rm Fe/H}]$ measurements with gas phase [O/H] measurements to infer the $\alpha$ -enhancement [59, 69, 36, e.g.,]. In a recent study, [58] applied this technique to massive star-forming galaxies at $z\approx 3.5$ , finding [O/Fe] $=0.425\pm 0.026$ for the average value of this mixed gas-stellar abundance ratio. These high redshift observations provide another direction to extend our modeling, and probing to early epochs may help break remaining degeneracies between yields and other GCE parameters. Applying the WAF one-zone models to their $z\approx 3.5$ data set, [58] find that explaining their high observed [O/Fe] ratios requires a high oxygen yield corresponding to [O/Fe] ${}_{\mathrm{cc}}\approx 0.7$ , a conclusion similar to but even stronger than the one inferred here from the ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ ratios of $z\sim 0$ and $z\sim 0.7$ ellipticals.

The other natural direction is to extend this work to model other element abundances. With SDSS and LEGA-C samples, we can obtain robust measurements for the mean abundances of up to a dozen elements at $z\sim 0$ and six elements at $z\sim 0.7$ [14, 5]. These include elements with different ratios of CCSN/SNIa enrichment (e.g., Si, Ca, Ni, Mn) and elements in which the delayed contribution comes from asymptotic giant branch (AGB) stars rather than SNIa (e.g., C, N, Sr, Ba). For all these elements, we would like to know whether their abundances in ellipticals can be explained by adopting stellar yields that reproduce Milky Way data combined with the GCE parameters inferred from Mg and Fe. The differing CCSN/SNIa ratios and the distinct DTD of AGB enrichment can further test the GCE models themselves.

## VI Conclusions

Massive quiescent galaxy populations exhibit well-defined trends of stellar age, $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]$ , and $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]$ with galaxy velocity dispersion or stellar mass. We have constructed one-zone GCE models with flexible star formation histories to interpret the trends measured by [5], who fit SSP models to the spectra of galaxies from the SDSS (at $z\approx 0$ ) and from LEGA-C (at $z\approx 0.7$ ). We predict SSP quantities from the light-weighted, logarithmically averaged quantities in the GCE model, denoted ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ , ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ , and ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ . Our tests with synthetic spectra from composite stellar populations show that this prediction is generally accurate, though the light-weighted ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ slightly exceeds the SSP age (by $\sim 0.5$ -2 Gyr) for the oldest galaxies (Figures 14, 19).

The components of our GCE models are the star formation history (SFH), the star formation efficiency timescale $\tau_{*}=M_{\rm gas}/\dot{M}_{*}$ , the outflow efficiency $\eta=\dot{M}_{\rm out}/\dot{M}_{*}$ , and the IMF-averaged Mg and Fe yields from CCSN and SNIa. Following 80, we normalize $y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm cc}$ using the [50] determination of the mean observed Fe yield of CCSN, choose $y_{\rm Mg}^{\rm cc}/y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm cc}$ based on the plateau of $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]$ seen in metal-poor Milky Way stars, and choose $y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm Ia}/y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm cc}$ so that GCE models with a continuous, slowly declining SFH evolve to $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]\approx 0$ at late times. We adopt $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}=0.45$ as our default value of the plateau, but we consider models with a higher $y_{\rm Mg}^{\rm cc}/y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm cc}$ corresponding to $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}=0.55$ .

With our adopted SFH parameterization (Equation 2), star formation begins at $t_{\rm start}$ , rises approximately linearly to a maximum at $t\approx\tau_{1}$ , then declines exponentially on a timescale $\tau_{2}$ and truncates sharply at a cutoff time $t_{\rm cut}$ , where the galaxy transitions to quiescence. Because our parameterization already allows a variety of rise times $\tau_{1}$ , we fix $t_{\rm start}=0.5\pm 0.5$ Gyr, assuming that star formation in massive ellipticals commences at $z\gtrsim 6$ . While all four SFH parameters affect the mean age and abundances, the trajectories of ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ vs. ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ and ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ vs. ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ are not sensitive to the individual values of $\tau_{1}$ , $\tau_{2}$ , and $t_{\rm cut}$ , and the value of $t_{\rm start}$ simply translates these trajectories in time (Figure 5). Thus, once the yields, $\tau_{*}$ , and $\eta$ are specified, the choice of SFH has surprisingly little leverage on the predicted ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ and ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ ratios for galaxies of a specified ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ .

Figure 11 summarizes the impact of GCE model parameters on ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ - ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ and ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ - ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ trajectories. Beyond the linear scaling of Mg abundance with $y_{\rm Mg}^{\rm cc}$ , the predicted ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ depends mainly on $\tau_{*}$ in old galaxies and on $\eta$ in younger galaxies: higher SFE (lower $\tau_{*}$ ) leads to more rapid early enrichment, while higher $\eta$ leads to greater metal loss and lower metallicity at later times. Several parameters affect the predicted ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ at fixed ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ , but only at the $\sim 0.02$ -dex level, and it is generally easier to decrease the predicted ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ than to increase it. Our fiducial models adopt a double-exponential DTD for SNIa that approximates a $t^{-1.1}$ power-law with a minimum delay time $t_{{\rm d,min}}=150$ Myr. If we reduce $t_{{\rm d,min}}$ to 50 Myr, predicted ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ ratios drop by $\sim 0.05$ dex because of the more rapid onset of SNIa Fe enrichment.

Figure 13 compares a representative set of GCE models to the SDSS and LEGA-C data. With reasonable parameter choices, the models can reproduce the observed ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ values, with the SDSS trend of higher ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ at higher $\sigma$ explained mainly by decreasing outflow efficiency (lower $\eta$ ) in deeper potential wells. Even with $\eta=0$ , reproducing the super-solar ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ observed in higher- $\sigma$ SDSS galaxies and all LEGA-C galaxies requires $y_{\rm Mg}^{\rm cc}$ to be $\sim 0.1$ dex higher than our default value, and a high SFE ( $\tau_{*}\sim 0.5$ Gyr) is needed for the oldest SDSS galaxies. The higher $y_{\rm Mg}^{\rm cc}$ is within the uncertainty estimated by 80, so we do not consider the high observed ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ to be problematic for our models. However, a bottom-heavy IMF in the most massive ellipticals [73, 15] would lower the $y_{\rm Mg}^{\rm cc}$ in these systems, making their high ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ more difficult to explain; shifting from a [39] IMF to a Salpeter-like IMF lowers $y_{\rm Mg}^{\rm cc}$ by 0.14 dex.

With our fiducial CCSN yield ratio of $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}=0.45$ , our models underpredict the observed ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ values at a given ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ by $\sim 0.08$ dex at $z=0$ and $\sim 0.05$ dex at $z=0.7$ . With the higher ratio $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}=0.55$ , the discrepancy with the data is smaller, though once we choose parameters to match ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}-{\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ the models still consistently underpredict the observed ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ (Figure 13bd). At $z=0.7$ the difference is comparable to the $1\sigma$ statistical uncertainties in the observed values, but at $z=0$ it is a statistically significant 0.05-0.07 dex in most velocity dispersion bins. Spectral fits imply that the observed stellar populations of ellipticals are old, but they are still young enough to allow ample time for SNIa Fe enrichment. Within the fairly flexible framework of our models, that SNIa enrichment should have depressed ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ below the observationally inferred values.

The tension between models and the data is mild enough that it might be explained by systematic uncertainties in the SSP spectral fits, e.g., from imperfect stellar libraries. Reducing the observational estimates of ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ by $\sim 0.05$ dex or increasing the estimated ages by 1-2 Gyr would align the data with our $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}=0.55$ models. Reducing ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ by 0.1 dex would remove the conflict with our $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}=0.45$ models.

Alternatively, this tension could be a sign that the IMF-averaged yields in elliptical galaxies are systematically different from the empirical estimates of 80, which are motivated by global statistics of CCSN and SNIa rates and by abundance trends in the Milky Way. Agreement with the observed $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]$ would be improved by increasing $y_{\rm Mg}^{\rm cc}/y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm cc}$ (above $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}=0.55$ ), or by decreasing $y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm Ia}/y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm cc}$ . For example, Figure 15 shows that a model with $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]_{\rm cc}=0.45$ and $y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm Ia}/y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm cc}$ reduced from 1.65 to 1.0 can reproduce the ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ - ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ trends from SDSS and LEGA-C. However, observations suggest a higher SNIa DTD normalization in galaxy clusters relative to the field [43], which would imply a higher $y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm Ia}/y_{\rm Fe}^{\rm cc}$ in ellipticals, not lower.

Agreement between models and data can also be improved by adding a self-enriching burst of star formation to the end of a galaxy’s smooth SFH, immediately before the transition to quiescence. This terminating burst reduces the light-weighted age, and it increases both ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ and ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ because self-enrichment in a short burst is dominated by CCSN. We have developed a simple, approximate model for the impact of these terminating bursts (Figures 16 and 17, Appendix B). Bursts that consume just the gas that remains after the smooth star formation can boost ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ at fixed ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ by $\sim 0.03$ dex, while also boosting ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ by $\sim 0.02-0.08$ dex. If the burst is fueled by accretion of a metal-poor, gas-rich companion, then the increase of ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ can be larger, while ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]\rangle}$ may increase, stay flat, or even drop because of the dilution of the pre-burst ISM. The importance of terminating bursts could be probed observationally by looking for correlations between residuals from the ${\langle[{\rm Mg}/{\rm Fe}]\rangle}$ - ${\langle{\rm age}\rangle}$ relation and spectral signatures of late star formation, going beyond the SSP-fitting techniques used here.

Our results suggest several directions for future work. One is to compare our model star formation histories to SED-based observational estimates, including investigating the frequency and magnitude of terminating bursts. A second is to apply our models to emerging observational results at higher redshift, which should include progenitors of some of the oldest low- $z$ quiescent populations. A third is to extend our analysis to other elements whose abundance can be estimated by full spectral fitting, including elements that have substantial contributions from intermediate-mass ABG stars. Our results also highlight the importance of sharpening empirical constraints on IMF-averaged yields, in the Milky Way and in other local galaxies.

Elliptical galaxies differ from disk galaxies in their star formation histories and potentially in their outflows and other galactic scale phenomena. Stellar yields are governed by stellar-scale astrophysics, including the IMF, the physics of supernova explosions and black hole populations, and binary populations that may affect massive star evolution and the SNIa DTD. Building on the framework developed here, we hope to learn whether galactic scale effects fully explain the distinctive abundance patterns of ellipticals, or whether these patterns also imply different stellar scale astrophysics in the progenitors of massive quiescent galaxies.

## Appendix A fanCE

fanCE (Flexible Analytic Chemical Evolution) [25] is an analytic one-zone chemical evolution code. It implements the Weinberg, Andrews, & Freudenburg (2017) analytic solution for a constant, exponential declining, or linear-exponential (delayed tau) star formation history. It also implements a flexible, two-parameter star formation history $\propto(1-e^{-t/\tau_{1}})\cdot e^{-t/\tau_{2}}$ , which rises linearly on a timescale $\tau_{1}$ and then falls exponentially on a timescale $\tau_{2}$ for $\tau_{2}>\tau_{1}>0$ .

We provide Python implementations of fanCE via https://github.com/nmgountanis/fanCE so that others can easily adapt them to interpret other galaxies or stellar populations or explore alternative assumptions. The source code for fanCE can be downloaded from GitHub and installed by running:

cd <path_to_installation>

git clone https://github.com/nmgountanis/fanCE

cd fanCE

pip install -e .

If you make use of this code, please cite [79] for the analytic solutions and Gountanis et al. (2024, this paper) for the code implementation. The reference for the default yield choices is [80].

## Appendix B Mean metallicity of burst stars

Our goal is to compute the mean metallicity of stars formed during a burst described by a “leaky box” chemical evolution model (Hartwick 31; Binney and Merrifield 8, section 5.3; WAF, section 3.5), which generalizes “closed box” evolution [65] to allow outflow. These models assume instantaneous enrichment and instantaneous recycling of stellar mass loss. For notational simplicity, we will consider a single element of mass fraction $Z$ and yield $y$ . The metallicity evolution of the leaky box model is

$$ Z(t)={y\over 1+\eta^{\prime}-r^{\prime}}\left[-\ln f_{g}(t)\right]~, $$

where

$$ f_{g}(t)=M_{g}(t)/M_{g,i} $$

is the ratio of the gas mass to the initial gas mass. We have denoted the outflow mass-loading by $\eta^{\prime}$ to emphasize that it may differ from the value $\eta$ that applies during pre-burst evolution, and we have denoted the recycling factor by $r^{\prime}$ because a burst may not last long enough for the full recycling factor $r$ to be applicable. If the initial gas metallicity is non-zero (as it is in our models), then the enrichment described by Equation (B1) is added to the initial abundance $Z_{i}$ at the start of the burst.

Because there is, by assumption, no ongoing gas accretion during the burst, mass conservation implies

$$ M_{g}(t)+(1-r^{\prime})M_{*,{\rm form}}(t)+\eta^{\prime}M_{*,{\rm form}}(t)=M_{g,i}~, $$

where

$$ M_{*,{\rm form}}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\dot{M}_{*}(t^{\prime})dt^{\prime} $$

is the mass of stars formed and multiplying by $(1-r^{\prime})$ gives the current stellar mass. Dividing by $M_{g,i}$ and rearranging yields

$$ f_{*}(t)\equiv{M_{*,{\rm form}}(t)\over M_{g,i}}={1-f_{g}(t)\over 1+\eta^{\prime}-r^{\prime}}~. $$

For small $\eta^{\prime}$ and $f_{g}$ , the value of $f_{*}$ can exceed one because recycled gas can be formed into new stars. Stars formed at time $t^{\prime}$ have metallicity $Z(t^{\prime})$ , so the mean metallicity of all stars formed up to time $t$ is

$$ \langle Z_{*}\rangle={\int_{0}^{t}Z(t^{\prime})\dot{M}_{*}(t^{\prime})dt^{\prime}\over\int_{0}^{t}\dot{M}_{*}(t^{\prime})dt^{\prime}}={\int_{0}^{f_{*}}Z(f_{*}^{\prime})df_{*}^{\prime}\over\int_{0}^{f_{*}}df_{*}^{\prime}}={\int_{1}^{f_{g}}Z(f_{g}^{\prime})df_{g}^{\prime}\over\int_{1}^{f_{g}}df_{g}^{\prime}}~, $$

where the last equality uses the fact that $df_{*}^{\prime}/df_{g}^{\prime}=-(1+\eta^{\prime}-r^{\prime})^{-1}$ is constant and therefore cancels between the numerator and denominator. Applying Equation (B1) and evaluating the integral yields the final result

$$ \langle Z_{*}\rangle={y\over 1+\eta^{\prime}-r^{\prime}}\left[1+{f_{g}\ln f_{g}\over 1-f_{g}}\right]~. $$

The factor $\left[1+{f_{g}\ln f_{g}\over 1-f_{g}}\right]$ grows from $\frac{1}{2}(1-f_{g})$ at early times, when $(1-f_{g})\ll 1$ , to unity at late times, when $f_{g}\ll 1$ .

Our terminating burst models are parameterized by a dilution factor $F_{D}$ and a final gas fraction $f_{g}$ . (Recall that $f_{g}$ is the ratio of the gas mass at the end of the burst to the gas mass at the start of the burst, not to the stellar mass.) At the end of smooth evolution the gas mass is $\tau_{*}\dot{M}_{*}$ , so the initial gas mass for the burst is $M_{g,i}=(1+F_{D})\tau_{*}\dot{M}_{*}$ . We assume that the accreted gas is much lower metallicity than that in the parent elliptical, so that the gas phase abundance of element X is reduced by a factor $(1+F_{D})$ . We therefore compute the impact of a burst on our elliptical galaxy models by adding, in the final timestep, a mass of stars

$$ M_{\rm burst}=\tau_{*}\dot{M}_{*}(1+F_{D}){1-f_{g}\over 1+\eta^{\prime}-r^{\prime}} $$

(cf. Equation (B5)), with abundances

$$ \bar{Z}_{X,{\rm burst}}={Z_{X}\over 1+F_{D}}+{y_{\rm X}^{\rm cc}\over 1+\eta^{\prime}-r^{\prime}}\left[1+{f_{g}\ln f_{g}\over 1-f_{g}}\right]~, $$

where X = Mg, Fe, and $Z_{X}$ is the ISM abundance at the last timestep before the burst. We assume that the burst is too short to allow significant SNIa iron production. We adopt $\eta^{\prime}=0$ to maximize the burst impact, and we adopt $r^{\prime}=0.3$ in place of $r=0.4$ to allow for a short burst duration. Our assumption that accreted gas has negligibly low metallicity could be adjusted by changing the $1+F_{D}$ dilution factor in the first term. For the values $f_{g}=0.3$ and $f_{g}=0.05$ used in our illustrative burst models, the factor $\left[1+{f_{g}\ln f_{g}\over 1-f_{g}}\right]$ is 0.484 and 0.842, respectively.

## Appendix C Testing the SSP assumption against mock observations

*Figure 19: Results from simple two-population CSP tests. The $y$ -axis shows the deviations between the best-fit SSP-equivalent stellar population properties and the adopted logarithmic light-weighted quantities. Left: Both populations have the same stellar age and [Mg/Fe], but they differ in [Mg/H] by 0.4 dex. The $x$ -axis represents [Mg/H] of the lower metallicity population. All dashed lines have [Mg/Fe] = 0, while all solid lines have [Mg/Fe] = 0.3. The low transparency solid line repeats the 3 Gyr case but averaging linear (Mg/H) rather than the logarithmic quantity [Mg/H]. Center: Both populations have the same stellar age and [Mg/H], but they differ in [Mg/Fe] by the amount listed on the $x$ -axis. In all cases, the lower [Mg/Fe] population has [Mg/Fe] = 0. All dashed lines have [Mg/H] = 0, while all solid lines have [Mg/H] = -0.5. The low transparency solid line repeats the 3 Gyr case with linear averaging of (Mg/Fe). Right: Both populations have the same [Mg/H] and [Mg/Fe] but differ in log Age by the amount listed on the x-axis. In all cases, the lowest age is log(age) = 0.4 (2.5 Gyr). The low transparency line repeats the solar abundance case but with linear rather than logarithmic age averaging. The gray line shows the same case but for the mass-weighted logarithmic age.*

The observational measurements from SDSS and LEGA-C are derived assuming the galaxies form in a single burst of star formation from the gas of a single metallicity and elemental abundance pattern. On the other hand, the chemical evolution models applied to these data have extended star formation and chemical histories. Here, we test whether there is significant systematic bias caused by our comparison of observed SSP-equivalent values and the GCE light-weighted ones.

We generate simple mock CSP spectra by combining two SSPs with different ages, metallicities, and abundance ratios. We then fit the CSPs with the same SSP models used in the LEGA-C and SDSS measurements. Finally, we compare these best-fit SSP-equivalent ages and abundances to the true light-weighted values from the underlying SSPs.

The results from the mock tests are shown in Figure 19. We show the effects of altering only one parameter at a time. In the left panel, we fix the stellar age and [Mg/Fe] of the two populations but shift [Mg/H] by 0.4 dex. The $x$ -axis represents [Mg/H] of the lower metallicity population. The solid (dashed) lines show the results when both populations have [Mg/Fe] fixed to 0.0 (0.4). The average $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]$ of these two populations matches the $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]$ of the SSP fit to within 0.02 dex in most cases, with larger deviations up to 0.05 dex for $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]_{\mathrm{lower}}=-0.8$ and $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]=0.0$ . Because the two populations have the same age and thus the same $L_{\rm V}/M$ , it does not matter whether we weight by mass or by light. However, it does matter whether we average the logarithmic quantity $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]$ or average (Mg/Fe) and then take the logarithm. The former logarithmic average better approximates the SSP result, while the linear average over-predicts the SSP $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]$ by $\sim 0.04$ dex, as illustrated by the low transparency blue line for the $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]=0.3$ , 5 Gyr case.

In the center panel, we vary the abundance ratio [Mg/Fe], fixing the lowest [Mg/Fe] population to [Mg/Fe] $=0$ . Again, we show cases where the population ages and [Mg/H] are fixed to different values. Even for an $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]$ difference of 0.3 dex between the two populations, the mean $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]$ matches the SSP fit to within $\sim 0.01$ dex. For $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]=-0.5$ , linear averaging of (Mg/Fe) leads to a less accurate prediction than directly averaging $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]$ , as shown by the low transparency line. For $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]=0.0$ , the bias of linear averaging is similar in magnitude but opposite in sign to that of logarithmic averaging.

In the right panel, we vary the ages of the populations but fix [Mg/H] and [Mg/Fe]. In all tests, the lowest age is set to 2.5 Gyr. The light-weighted average of log(age) slightly overpredicts the log(age) of the SSP fit, by up to $\sim 0.1$ dex for a $\Delta\mathrm{log(age)}=0.7$ dex between the populations. Linear averaging of ages roughly doubles the error in predicting the SSP age, as illustrated by the low transparency line for the Solar abundance case. The $L_{\rm V}/M$ for the young and old populations differs, and mass-weighted averages give much less accurate predictions of the SSP age as expected (dashed line).

In other tests, we find that the slight age bias shown in Figure 19 becomes progressively stronger when the youngest SSP has a younger age ( $\leq$ 1 Gyr), because the A-star-dominated SSP has very strong Balmer absorption features that dramatically outshines the older stellar populations. This bias at young ages, however, is not an issue in this study, as the SDSS and LEGA-C populations are selected to be (often much) older than 1 Gyr.

The results of these tests agree with what has been previously found by Serra and Trager [54]; light-weighted abundances and abundance ratios are well approximated by SSP-equivalent measurements, whereas the stellar ages can be biased towards the youngest SSP. These two-population tests support our adopted procedure of predicting light-weighted $[{\rm Mg}/{\rm H}]$ , $[{\rm Mg/Fe}]$ , and log(age) values from our continuous models to compare to SSP observational results. We present an end-to-end test for representative continuous models in Section IV.2 (Figure 14).
